styles.name: Ballpoint Notebook
styles.brief: The direct evolution of the ORIGINAL style. Blue/black ballpoint lines on ruled or graph notebook paper, red margin line. Characters stay stick-figure-like box-head painters with the flat-cap hat (as in the original), but drawn with confident, wobbly, hand-inked lines and a little cross-hatching. Platforms are pen-ruled boxes with hatching. The ONLY saturated colour in the world is team paint, which looks like real wet paint/marker splashed onto the page. Think "game drawn in the back of an exercise book" — intentional, charming, coherent.
styles.one_liner: ColourWars drawn in the back of an exercise book: wobbly blue-ballpoint ledges with hatched faces on cream ruled paper with a red margin, black-ink box-head painters in flat caps, and team paint as the only real colour on the page, glossy and dripping off the platform edges.
styles.ownable: It grows straight out of the author's own MS-Paint stick figures. The box head, dot eyes, flat mouth, flat cap with brim, rectangle body and single-line limbs are all kept, just inked with confidence, so it is the original identity grown up rather than swapped out. The rule "ink and paper are colourless, only paint has colour" ties the look to the game's main mechanic: the score is the only saturated thing on screen, so coverage reads at a glance. Players have no ready comparison for it the way they do for pixel art. Small touches give it a personality nobody else has: punched holes, the red margin, faint pencil sums ("7 x 8 = 54 56"), a scribbled sun, "level 3 ?? more ledges".
styles.self:
What came out well:
- The medium reads at once: notebook paper, ballpoint hatching, marker-coloured clothing and glossy dripping paint.
- The two team colours stand apart sharply from a colourless world. In the 480x270 quarter-pane test the paint coverage is the most legible thing on screen, which suits a game scored by coverage.
- The characters are clearly the original box-head flat-cap painters, now with charm and readable poses. The sheet's idle/run/jump poses in blue and orange, plus pink/green/yellow, show the tint regions cleanly.

Weaknesses:
- At real in-game scale (~115 px tall, 3 px lines) the stick figures are thin. At quarter-pane size they shrink to small coloured tokens; the cap and body colour carry them, not the faces or limbs. A shipped version would want slightly heavier character lines than world lines, or a paper-white halo.
- The roller head is a simple rounded box that reads as a block more than a cylinder.
- The sprayer's gun body is a bit crude, though crude is arguably on-brief.
- The procedural wobble is fairly uniform. Real hand-inked lines vary in pressure and confidence more than this, and line weight barely varies at all.
- Being a static frame, the concept cannot show what a style like this would need in motion (boiled lines, smear frames).
- Yellow team paint on cream paper will have lower contrast than the other pairs, so it needs a darker rim in production.

Files, in the session scratchpad, concepts/doodle/:
- scene.svg (~259 KB), scene.png, scene_small.png
- character.svg (~140 KB), character.png
- gen.py (the generator)
styles.anim: The style is well suited to cheap animation. Stick limbs and a box head allow either a simple bone/cutout rig (limbs as single line segments, so there is no deformation problem) or a handful of hand-drawn frames per pose. A boil of 2-3 redrawn frames per pose on a 6-8 fps cycle would do most of the "living ink" work and also hide stiffness. Smear frames and dashed speed lines (already in the scene) are on-brief and cheap. The cost is that boil multiplies frame count by 2-3 for every tinted mask too. A shader-driven wobble (vertex or UV noise on line sprites, stepped at a low rate) could fake boil with zero extra art. Paint drips can be small spawned sprites at platform edges and need no per-character work.
styles.engine: The fit is very good. The characters are already split into a colourless ink layer plus flat tint regions (cap, overalls, tank, roller sleeve), so the engine's grayscale-mask team tinting at draw time maps directly. The "only paint has colour" rule means no other tinted asset can clash. Paint coverage as a runtime-painted surface layer suits it, but the glossy wet look (dark rim plus specular highlight) needs either a small shader pass over the paint mask (rim from an alpha-gradient/edge detect, a highlight from blurred-alpha normals) or baked gloss in tiling paint-band sprites. Drips are separate spawned sprites. The paper wants a camera-locked or slow-parallax tiled texture with its own rule lines. Platform hatching can be a tiling, world-space-aligned hatch texture clipped to the platform rect, so level geometry stays data-driven boxes. One engine concern: blue team paint over blue-ink outlines needs the paint layer drawn under or beside the ink edge, or blue loses its edge.
strengths: It grows straight out of the author's own box-head flat-cap stick figures, so the identity is kept and matured rather than replaced. This is the strongest argument for it.
"Ink and paper are colourless, only paint has colour" is a real art-direction rule tied to the scoring mechanic. Coverage is the loudest thing on screen in the full frame.
Cheap and forgiving for a solo non-artist: wobble and roughness read as intentional, and level geometry is just hatched boxes.
Character tint regions are cleanly separated, and the pink/green/yellow variants on the sheet show the mask approach works.
Notebook details (margin, punched holes, pencil sums, 'level 3 ?? more ledges') give it charm and a humour that pixel art cannot easily match.
risks: Blue team paint against blue-ballpoint world ink. Every platform edge is navy, so blue coverage partly merges with outlines, especially at quarter-pane. Blue/yellow and blue/orange matches always have a blue team. Consider black or graphite world ink, or keep ink strictly under/behind the paint.

The characters are too thin at real scale. At 480x270 they are small coloured tokens and the faces and limbs vanish. They need heavier character lines than world lines, a paper-white halo, or a larger character-to-world ratio.
Yellow (and to a lesser degree green) paint on cream paper will lose contrast. It needs a darkened rim or an ink outline on paint bands.
The scene is sparse. Large empty paper areas look like an unfinished level rather than intentional minimalism, and the background needs more mid-ground doodles at low contrast without adding noise.

The 'doodle on notebook paper' look is common in mobile/Flash games (Doodle Jump and its imitators), so it can read as cheap or casual unless the line quality and paint gloss are clearly better than the clones.
The procedural wobble is uniform with no line-weight variation. Shipped art drawn this way can look machine-made. Hand-drawn or pressure-varied lines would raise it a lot.
Hatched wall faces and the paper grain become a mid-grey shimmer when scaled down, which can moire in motion at small pane sizes.
styles.verdict: This is the right direction for this author: it keeps the original MS-Paint identity, is cheap to produce, and its "only paint is coloured" rule serves the scoring mechanic directly. The execution is a solid 7 but has two real flaws. Blue paint fights the blue ballpoint ink, and the characters dissolve into small tokens at quarter-pane. Both can be fixed (graphite or black world ink, heavier character lines with a paper halo) without changing the style. Its potential is higher than this frame shows, and its comparison bar is far lower than the 16-bit pixel candidate's, as long as the line quality stays clearly above Doodle Jump-clone level.

identity.reason: The exercise-book framing is a natural evolution of the box-head painter. The pencil sums and the 'level 3 ?? more ledges' note give it humour that pixel art cannot copy. In the render, blue paint really does merge into the blue-ballpoint platform outlines, and at quarter-pane size the figures become small tokens. It also sits close to the crowded Doodle Jump look.

production.reason: About as cheap and forgiving as mspaint, and the identity carries over directly. At quarter pane, though, blue paint really does merge into the blue-ballpoint outlines, the figures shrink to specks, and the sparse page reads as empty. Its gloss/rim look also wants a shader. Switching to graphite or black ink and heavier character lines fixes most of it.

player.reason: Charming, but blue paint merges with the blue ballpoint outlines and thin platforms. The figures become tokens, and the cream paper weakens yellow.

styles.name: Paint.exe Maximalism
styles.brief: Embrace the original MS-Paint origin as a deliberate aesthetic (not pixel art — pixel art is crafted; this is CRUDE and proud of it). Aliased 1-px-ish pencil-tool lines, airbrush-tool speckle sprays, bucket-fill flats with gaps, the default 28-colour palette energy, white canvas, slightly-off rectangles drawn by mouse. Characters are the original box-head hat stick figures, faithfully crude. A game about paint, made in Paint. Make it look intentional and funny rather than unfinished.
styles.one_liner: A game about paint, made in Paint: the original box-head flat-cap stick painters, drawn in jagged pencil lines and filled with a bucket that misses a few pixels, spray and roll thick, drippy brush-tool paint across grey slabs on a white canvas whose background doodles quietly joke about themselves.
styles.ownable: It comes straight from the author's original art (box head, two dot eyes, a one-line mouth, flat cap with a brim, rectangle body, single-line limbs), so it is a continuation and not a reskin. Nobody can compare it to a better version because nobody else makes deliberate MS Paint art for a shipped game. The medium is also the theme: the tools the game is about (spray, roll, bucket) are the tools the art is made with. The airbrush tool literally is the sprayer's mist, and the bucket fill is the team colour. Its signature details are repeatable rules, not one-off flourishes: aliased staircase lines, white pixel gaps where the bucket fill didn't reach, square-pixel airbrush speckle, and paint drawn as a lumpy brush-tool band with hanging drips. The backdrop gags (a cloud left inside a dashed selection box labelled "^ do not move this cloud", a sun with an eraser bite out of one ray, a WET sign) make the crudeness read as intentional and funny. The look is also cheap to produce: any team member can author new art in this style with the tools they already have.
styles.self:
What works: the medium is convincing and clearly not pixel art. The players are honestly scaled at about 120px in the 900px frame. In the 480x270 quarter-pane test, the team colours on the players and especially the paint on surfaces stand out strongly against white and light grey. The background stays quiet because it is all pale pencil, and the jokes come across as intentional rather than unfinished. In the scene, about 50% of the walkable tops are painted (blue on the left floor, the left platform, the landing zone and half the top platform; orange on platform B, the ramp, the step and the right floor), and the floor reads as the score.

Weaknesses:
- At quarter scale the stick figures are thin. Their faces and limbs dissolve, and they read mostly as a coloured cap and shirt with a weapon. That is enough for gameplay, but it has little charm at that size.
- The sprayer hold is still a bit clumsy: the tank overlaps the torso. In the sheet's jump pose the tucked legs read awkwardly.
- The "maximalism" is restrained on purpose so the background does not compete. Someone expecting a busy, loud Paint collage will find the scene sparse. The jokes are the maximal part, not the density.
- The style's risk is that crude can look low-effort to players. Its success depends on consistent rules (the speckle, the bucket gaps, the drips) and on the jokes in the environment, and these concepts only hint at how that would hold across a whole game and its animation.
- The roller sleeve is drawn as a flat rectangle, which reads as a box more than a cylinder.
comps: Kingdom of Loathing / West of Loathing
styles.anim: The style suits limbs drawn as single lines, so a cheap rig or frame-by-frame at a low frame rate (8-12 fps) fits it, and a crude 2-3 frame cycle reads as a joke, not as a flaw. Line boil (re-jittering the pencil lines each frame) would make the art feel alive almost for free. Watch out for one thing: the staircase aliasing only holds at integer scale with no rotation. A weapon rotating to follow the aim angle will resample, blur or shimmer unless you pre-render the angles or use nearest-neighbour sampling. Paint needs drips that grow over time and brush-stamp tiles. The airbrush mist should be a particle that scatters square pixels. All of these are cheap.
styles.engine: This fits the engine very well. The team colour is only flat fills on the cap, shirt, tank window, nozzle and roller sleeve, so it maps cleanly onto a grayscale mask that is tinted at draw time. Surface paint can be stamped at runtime as an irregular band from tiled brush stamps plus drip sprites, with no shader needed. Requirements: point sampling, integer scaling or exact-size draws per pane, and no sub-pixel camera smoothing that blurs the aliased edges. Snap the camera to the pixel grid. The style needs no paper-texture or halftone shader, because the white canvas is the texture. One gap: the team colours need per-pair checks against the light-grey slabs and the white background. Yellow (in the blue/yellow draw) on light grey or white will be weak, and the backdrop sun is already yellow.
strengths: It continues the author's own original box-head flat-cap figures, so it is owned rather than a borrowed genre look.
The medium is the theme: the airbrush tool is the sprayer's mist and the bucket fill is the team colour, which makes a strong pitch hook.
Painted surface reads as the score immediately. The thick drippy bands on grey slabs are the loudest thing in the frame, even at quarter-pane size.
The background stays quiet in pale pencil, and its gags (the 'do not move this cloud' selection box, the WET sign, the PAINT can) make the crudeness read as deliberate.
Cheapest possible production for a solo non-artist: anyone can author new assets in a raster editor, and it is hard to compare it to a 'better' version.
The repeatable rules (staircase lines, bucket-fill gaps, square-pixel speckle, drips) give it a style guide you can actually maintain.
risks: Crude can read as low-effort in store screenshots and trailers. The charm depends on the jokes and consistent rules, and a static capsule image may not carry them.
At quarter-pane size the players shrink to a coloured cap, a shirt and a weapon. Faces and limbs dissolve, so player identity and charm drop exactly where 4-player split-screen lives.

Yellow (in the blue/yellow pair) on light-grey slabs and the white canvas will be low contrast, and it clashes with the yellow sun. The concept only proves blue/orange in the scene, and pink/green/yellow are untested on surfaces.
The overpainted swatch already looks muddy. Contested areas with interleaved drips may become hard to read.
Rotation and fractional scaling break the aliased look, which constrains weapon aiming, camera zoom and any juice effects.
The 'maximalism' in the name is not delivered: the scene is sparse. If the author wants a loud, dense MS Paint collage, this is a different, quieter direction.
There are small execution flaws: the sprayer tank overlaps the torso, the jump legs are awkward, the roller reads as a box, and the vertical hang-lines cut through clouds and add clutter.
styles.verdict: This is the most defensible direction for this author. It is his own art grown into a set of rules, cheap to produce, and the paint-as-score readability is genuinely good. The execution is a solid proof of concept, not a finished look: it proves blue/orange on white and grey but not yellow, and the figures lose all charm at quarter-pane size, so the next pass should thicken limbs and faces at 1x and test every colour pair. The style's ceiling depends on writing and consistency more than on rendering skill, which suits a solo developer, but it will live or die on whether screenshots read as a joke rather than as unfinished.

identity.reason: This is the purest continuation of the original, and gags like 'do not move this cloud', WET and PAINT make the crudeness read as deliberate. The small render reads well, and paint on grey slabs is loud. The risk is store screenshots that look unfinished, plus yellow against the white canvas and the sun. The identity is right, but there is no crafted counterweight to make it read as intentional at first glance. That counterweight is what the riso mix adds.

production.reason: Best production profile I looked at. The 480x270 render is the cleanest of all: thick drippy bands on grey slabs, white canvas, no grain to shimmer. Paint is flat fills with drip sprites, so nothing depends on a gloss or halftone shader. Assets can be made in any raster editor, rough execution reads as the joke, and four or more arenas are just slabs plus a few gag props. Risks: it can read as unfinished in screenshots, aliased weapons resample badly when rotated, and yellow is weak on white and grey.

player.reason: Paint coverage is very legible against white and grey, and the jokes give it charm. The figures are hairline sticks in a quarter pane, and as a capsule it risks looking unfinished. Yellow on white fails.

styles.name: Risograph Print
styles.brief: Two- or three-drum risograph print: limited inks (e.g. a navy/charcoal key ink + paper), visible halftone dots, slight misregistration between ink layers, paper grain. Team paint printed as the fluoro/spot ink layers. Note the game menu art already uses halftone + dry-brush splatter on dark navy with orange/teal, so this direction connects to existing assets.
styles.one_liner: A three-drum risograph print: the original box-headed, flat-capped stick painter drawn in a navy key ink on warm paper, with team paint as the only fluoro spot ink in the frame, laid down as slightly misregistered blue and orange that drips off solid navy plank shelves.
styles.ownable: It keeps the author's own MS-Paint character exactly as built: a box head, two dot eyes, a flat line mouth, a flat cap with a brim, a rectangular body and single-line limbs. The style changes the print process, not the character, so the identity stays and the crude drawing now reads as a deliberate graphic choice. Players have no ready comparison for a risograph game, the way they do for pixel art. The ink system also does gameplay work. Navy key plus paper is the whole world, and the team colours are the only spot inks, so anything bright on screen is either a player or the score. A random colour draw is a drum swap (pink/green and yellow are shown on the sheet). The look also connects to the existing menu art: halftone, splatter and navy with orange/teal.
styles.self:
**What works:** the medium is convincing at full size. Halftone, speckle, banding, misregistration and overprint all read as a printed object, not a flat vector. At the 480x270 split-pane test, the paint is the most saturated thing in the frame and the score is readable at a glance. Blue on the left and lower floor and orange across the mid shelf, the step and the ramp read as clear territories, and the drips over solid navy plank faces are very legible. The sheet shows the character idea well: the same crude painter in each team's ink, plus five ink-colour versions at 1:1 scale against the 52x120 collision box.

**Weaknesses:**
- **Characters are tiny at honest scale.** At 480x270 a player is about a 35-pixel mark. You can tell which team is where, but the painter's personality (face, cap brim) is lost.
- **Tangled arms.** On the run poses, both stick arms cross the body to reach the weapon and create a small knot of navy lines where the clarity of the original figure suffered.
- **Plain weapons.** The large sprayer (a gun with a canister on top) and the roller are functional but plain, without much design charm.
- **Background.** The large window frame is the most prominent background element and slightly too graphic. The ladder and the tin shelf are generic workshop dressing.
- **Banding on large areas.** The riso streak noise on large dark areas (the floor block) can read as scan or compression artifacting rather than ink.
- **Paint-over is not shown.** The concept doesn't solve how one team's paint replaces the other's. Overprinting two spot inks would mix them into a muddy colour, so the game would have to knock out the old team's paint and treat the inks as exclusive, unlike real riso.
- **Animation is untested.** Whether the halftone and grain shimmer during scrolling or animation is the big unknown.
comps: Splatoon (unavoidable for the paint/territory mechanic, not the look)
Return of the Obra Dinn (the best-known game whose identity is a print/dither process)
Pentiment (print and woodcut process as style)
West of Loathing / Kingdom of Loathing (crude stick figures used on purpose)
Stick Fight: The Game (local stick-figure brawler)
Duck Game (local split-screen arena, minimal figures)
risograph zines and poster art in general, rather than any one game
styles.anim: The characters are a box body, a box head, a cap and single-line limbs. That makes a cheap cutout or bone rig, or a few hand-drawn frames per state; three-frame idle/run/jump sets are believable for one person. The riso texture (speckle, edge wobble) should be a shader rather than baked into frames. Done that way, boiling the noise seed at about 8-12 fps gives a "line boil" that comes for free and hides crude in-betweens. Baking texture per frame would flicker randomly and double the work. The tangled run-pose arms on the sheet show the real animation risk: with stick limbs, every weapon pose needs deliberate arm placement, or the silhouette becomes a knot at game scale. Misregistration has to stay a fixed per-layer offset. If it jitters per frame it reads as a rendering bug.
styles.engine: Fits a tint-the-grayscale-mask engine well. The design is already two channels: a key-ink sprite in fixed navy, plus a spot-ink mask tinted with the team colour at draw time. Drawing the tinted layer with a small UV/position offset gives misregistration for one extra draw. Runtime paint fits too: render the coverage mask, tint it, then multiply by a tiling ink-speckle/banding texture and a jagged-edge threshold. Drips can be a cheap vertical extrusion in the paint shader or decal stamps at plank edges. Shader needs: (1) a fullscreen paper-grain multiply overlay; (2) a halftone for wall, shadow and floor tones; (3) multiply blending for overprint on knockouts. The open decision is the halftone space. Screen-locked dots make a "shower door" swim when the camera scrolls. World-locked dots can moiré when a quarter pane shows the world at a different scale. Pick dot size per pane resolution and test early. Paint-over has to be exclusive replacement, not a real overprint of two inks, which suits a coverage-mask model anyway.
strengths: It keeps the author's own box-head, flat-cap painter and changes only the printing, so the crude drawing reads as a deliberate graphic choice instead of 'programmer art'. This directly answers the fear that pixel art is generic.

The ink rule works for gameplay: the world is navy key ink on paper, and the team inks are the only saturated colour. Anything bright is either a player or the score. At 480x270 the paint is the first thing you see.
Paint on solid navy planks, with drips running off the edges, has excellent contrast, and the drips make coverage readable at a glance.
It ties directly to the existing menu art (halftone, splatter, navy with orange/teal), so the gameplay and UI can share one visual language.
Production is cheap and forgiving for a non-artist: stick figures, flat platforms and procedural texture, where roughness reads as part of the medium.
Random team pairs fit naturally as 'drum swaps'. The sheet shows that pink/green and blue/yellow work on the figures.
risks: The characters are too small and too thin at quarter-pane scale. The players are about 35 px tall, the face and cap are lost, and the single-line limbs almost disappear into the dotted wall. The paper halo helps, but the figures need thicker key lines, or the camera needs to come closer.

The dense, even halftone wall covers the whole background. It flattens into a grey buzz at small size and is the most likely thing to swim or moiré while scrolling or in four panes. This is untested and is the main technical unknown.

Yellow (and probably light green) team ink on cream paper has weak contrast, both for the characters and for paint not on a navy surface. The blue/yellow pair needs a darker yellow or a key outline around the paint.

Background props are weak. The window grid is the boldest background shape and competes with the platforms. The shelves of tins and the ladder at right and left are faint generic filler. The wall needs fewer, softer props.
The large navy floor block has streak/banding noise that reads as compression artifacts, and so much solid key ink weighs the bottom of the frame down.
On the run poses the arms cross the body to reach the weapons, which blurs the most important silhouette. The weapons themselves are plain.
The concept never shows one team's paint replacing the other's. Real overprint would make mud, so the inks must be exclusive, which quietly breaks the 'real riso' fiction where colours meet.
styles.verdict: The execution is good: the full-size scene really reads as a printed object, the paint-versus-world separation is the best a paint game could ask for, and it keeps the author's own crude painter with its identity intact. It falls short where it matters most at real split-screen size: the stick figures are too thin and small, and the busy halftone wall turns into noise. The fix is thicker key lines and a quieter wall, not a different style. As a direction it is distinctive, cheap for a solo developer, rarely seen in games, and forgiving of rough execution. That makes it a stronger bet than detailed 16-bit pixel art, provided the scrolling halftone and the yellow pairing are prototyped early.

identity.reason: The world rule is excellent: only the spot inks are saturated, and paint on solid navy planks with drips reads very well. It also connects to the menu art. It ranks below the mix because it changes the figure, giving it team-coloured bodies and a sketchier navy line, so it is less obviously his painter. In the small render the even halftone wall turns into a grey buzz, and the window grid competes with the platforms.

production.reason: Cheap to author: navy key sprite plus tint mask, and misregistration costs one offset draw. Paint on navy planks is excellent. The production unknown is a halftone wall that swims or moirés when scrolling and across pane sizes; at small size it already becomes a grey buzz. That needs an early prototype.

player.reason: Paint on navy planks reads well, and the drips sell the score. It also ties into the existing menu art, which helps the UI pass come later. The figures are thin at quarter size, and the full-wall halftone becomes a grey buzz that will likely shimmer in four panes.

styles.name: Ink Wash
styles.brief: Black sumi brush ink on warm rice paper. World and characters are monochrome brush strokes with dry-brush edges and ink washes for depth. Team paint is the only colour and reads as shockingly saturated against the monochrome — coverage instantly legible. Painter characters as expressive brush gestures.
styles.one_liner: Box-headed painters drawn in loaded black sumi strokes on warm rice paper, under faint misted mountains and an ensō sun. The only colour on screen is team paint, flat and fully saturated, sitting on ledges that are each a single brushstroke.
styles.ownable: It keeps the original game's identity instead of replacing it. The box head with two dot eyes, the flat mouth and the flat cap are all still there, now drawn as brush gestures (a fat dry-brush torso, single-stroke limbs, a square head outlined in one brush loop). An ink-wash platformer where colour exists only as team paint has no obvious comparison the way 16-bit pixel art does. The colour rule is also the scoring rule: every pixel of colour belongs to a team, so coverage reads at a glance without any UI. The tintable regions are cleanly separate on a monochrome body (cap crown, trailing scarf, sprayer reservoir, roller sleeve), so the runtime tint system gets clean masks for free. A scarf flowing behind each figure gives a large, readable flag of team colour even at quarter-pane size.
styles.self:
What came out well:
- **Hierarchy.** At 480x270 the two players and all the paint jump out from the beige and grey world, and coverage is easy to read from the colour alone.
- **Ledges.** These are the strongest part. Each is a single loaded horizontal stroke with dry-brush tails and a darker-edged wash beneath, and they look properly brushed.
- **Characters.** The dry-brush streaks in the torsos sell the brush on the character sheet. The box-head homage gives the figures charm and keeps a continuity with the author's original art.

Weaknesses:
- **Figures at scale.** At honest in-game scale (about 112 px) they read as small and fairly thin. Most of their recognisability comes from the cap, the scarf and the white face square, not the brushwork, which mostly disappears below about 60 px.
- **Medium.** It reads as convincing digital sumi rather than real ink on paper: the strokes are cleaner and more uniform than a real brush, and the procedural grain is a bit regular.
- **Background details.** The mountains are still somewhat cone-shaped and generic. The pine bough and ensō are serviceable, not beautiful.
- **Weapons.** The sprayer and roller are crude; the large roller's handle-to-frame join is awkward, and the sprayer's hose loop is unclear.
- **Splats.** These need hand art; at the moment they are spiky procedural blobs.
- **Hidden risks.** The concept doesn't show how motion would look: brush-stroke animation can easily look like jittery tracing. A screen this restrained may also feel sparse over a whole match.

Revisions:
- Cut the speckled ink texture back to sparse, direction-aware dry streaks.
- Removed the stripy paper fibres.
- Made the mountains subtler and banded them with mist so the lower play area stays clean.
- Thickened the figures and rounded the caps.
- Moved the sprayer tank off the face.
- Raised gravity on the spray arc so it lands on its own splat.
- Joined the roller trail to the roller, and fixed the roller sleeve floating above the ground.
- Fixed an encoding bug that blanked the character sheet.

The final files, all in the session scratchpad, concepts/sumi/, are scene.svg (188 KB) and character.svg (281 KB), with scene.png, scene_small.png and character.png rendered from those final SVGs.
comps: Okami (sumi-e brush world, the default reference anyone will reach for)
Ink (Zack Bell, 2014): a minimalist platformer where splashed colour reveals the level, the closest mechanical-plus-visual cousin
Splatoon (paint-coverage scoring, which the game already follows)
Inkulinati (ink-on-parchment 2D, though medieval rather than East Asian)
Limbo / Shadow Fight (monochrome silhouette figures with sparse accents)
Gris (watercolour platformer where colour is the payoff)
styles.anim: The figures are simple: a black torso slab, single-stroke limbs and a box head. That suits a cutout or skeletal rig (Spine, DragonBones, or the engine's own sprite parts), with a small library of scanned brush strokes swapped per limb. A 3-4 frame stroke swap or a slight boil on edges would sell 'hand-inked' cheaply; a full frame-by-frame redraw of brush strokes is where cost and jitter risk explode. The scarf is the one element that needs secondary motion, and a 3-5 segment verlet strip handles it cheaply. Paint drips, splats and the ensō can be tweened decals. The concept does not show any motion, so the claim that 'brush-stroke animation looks like jittery tracing' is untested. A rigid rig would make the figures look like puppets, which is acceptable at this crude, charming level.
styles.engine: Excellent fit with the tint system. The character body is pure monochrome, and the tint regions (cap, scarf, sprayer reservoir, roller sleeve) are spatially separate, so the grayscale team masks are trivial and the pink/green and blue/yellow swaps on the sheet already work. Runtime surface painting also fits: paint is meant to be flat saturated fill on a near-black ledge stroke, so it needs no lighting or texture match, and a flat-colour mask with a slight edge-noise or drip decal is enough. Shader needs are modest: a screen-space paper-grain multiply overlay (one tiled texture), optional low-amplitude UV noise on paint edges, and pre-rendered wash or mountain parallax layers. Do not port the SVG feTurbulence or displacement filters to runtime; bake them into sprites. One caveat: the paper overlay must not multiply over the paint, or paint loses its 'different material' punch, so draw paint after the paper pass or exclude it from that pass.
strengths: Paint contrast is the best I would expect from any style here. Colour exists only as team paint, so coverage reads instantly at both 1600x900 and 480x270 with no UI, and the art rule and the scoring rule are the same rule.

Ledges as single loaded horizontal brushstrokes, with dark-edged washes beneath, are genuinely good and give paint a near-black base, which maximises saturation for all three colour pairs (yellow and green included).
It keeps the author's box-head, dot-eye, flat-cap identity rather than replacing it. The crude figure now reads as deliberate brush gesture instead of MS Paint.
Roughness is forgiving: wobbly, imperfect strokes read as medium, not incompetence, which suits a non-artist working with a real brush and a scanner.
Tint regions are clean and separate on a monochrome body, and the trailing scarf is a large readable team flag at quarter-pane size.
The comparison field is thin. Okami is the obvious reference, but no well-known side-view ink-wash shooter exists, unlike 16-bit pixel art.
risks: The execution reads as digital marker or vector-with-noise rather than sumi. The scratchy streak texture is regular and uniform across every stroke, and the torsos look like hatched black slabs, not 'expressive brush gestures'. Players who know Okami will notice.

The figures are small and thin at in-game scale. At 480x270 they come down to cap, scarf and a white face square; the brushwork vanishes and the figure is close to a stick-figure silhouette. Fine for identity, but they do not read as painterly.
Backgrounds are generic: cone mountains, a stock ensō and a pine bough are the first three sumi clichés. A full match of this risks feeling sparse and samey across stages.

The paper is warm beige. Yellow and orange paint on bare paper (off-ledge splatter, projectiles in the air) has much weaker contrast than on ink, and the scene shows orange spray dots almost disappearing against the beige.

The odd L-shaped ledge joint at right reads as a mistake rather than a design, a sign that level geometry (walls, slopes, ceilings) has not been worked out in this language. Vertical and underside surfaces must also hold paint and still look brushed.
Weapons are crude (the sprayer's hose loop is unclear, the roller handle join is awkward), and splats are spiky procedural blobs that need hand art.
Motion is unproven. Brush-stroke characters animated badly look like jittery tracing or stiff puppets.
Production requires a scanned-stroke library and baking. The procedural SVG approach does not transfer to runtime, so the real pipeline is still to be built.
styles.verdict: This is the strongest concept on the scoring-readability axis: monochrome ink with colour reserved for team paint is a style rule that makes coverage legible at a glance, it fits the tint-mask engine almost perfectly, and it keeps the author's box-head identity instead of throwing it away. The execution is only middling. It reads as digital marker with a noise filter rather than real sumi, the figures lose their brushwork below about 60 px, and the backdrop is a stack of ink-wash clichés. The style's potential is clearly higher than this concept, and much of the gap could be closed by a non-artist with a real brush, a scanner and a stroke library, which makes it a credible solo-dev direction with a lower comparison bar than 16-bit pixel art.

identity.reason: It has the best paint contrast and keeps the box-head look (now with a scarf). In the render it reads as digital marker, and the backdrop is the usual sumi clichés: cone mountains, an ensō and a pine bough. The odd L-shaped ledge shows that level geometry has not been worked out in this language.

production.reason: Paint contrast is excellent, but it needs a scanned-stroke library and baking. The execution reads as digital marker, and the comparison to Okami raises the bar.

player.reason: A clean read where paint is the only colour. The ink-black ledges give paint a dark base, and the scarf works as a team flag. The figures are thin specks in a quarter pane, and the frame is too quiet for a capsule.

styles.name: Drafting Table
styles.brief: The world is a technical drawing on off-white drafting paper / vellum: graphite construction lines, dimension arrows and annotations, hatching for section cuts, title-block corner. Characters are drafting mannequins or architects-sketch figures. Avoid blue background (blue is a team colour). Team paint lands on the drawing as real paint.
styles.one_liner: The arena is a graphite section drawing on warm drafting paper. Hatched slabs, datum markers and dimension arrows set the stage, and glossy, dripping team paint lands on it like a real spill on an architect's sheet. The painters are drafting mannequins that keep the original game's box head and flat cap.
styles.ownable: There is no ready comparison for it. Players have seen many pixel workshops, but very few have played inside a technical drawing. The style has a clear grammar of its own. Platforms are section cuts with 45-degree hatching (cross-hatch on the high deck), and the ground uses the concrete section symbol of dots and triangles. Lines overshoot at the corners, construction lines run off the slab edges, and hidden support posts are dashed. Elevation datum triangles (+2.20, +3.10), dimension strings, a centre-line mark, a section callout, a title block and drafting tape sit on the sheet. The paint breaks every drafting convention: it is the only saturated, glossy, wet material on the page, so the score layer and the world can never be confused. The characters stay close to the author's MS-Paint identity. They keep the box head, two dot eyes, flat mouth, brimmed flat cap and single-line limbs, now re-drawn as drafting mannequins with white joint circles at the knees and elbows, a dash-dot centre line, and a smock in team colour. It reads as a grown-up version of the original game, not a replacement. The world can also be extended without new art skills: more drafting conventions (stairs in section, revision clouds, north arrows, erased lines) give new level vocabulary.
styles.self:
What works:
- The medium reads right away: warm paper, hatched section slabs, dimension strings, datum markers and a title block. Nothing else in the batch looks like it.
- Paint is the only saturated, glossy thing in the frame, so in the 480x270 split-pane test the blue and orange coverage on surfaces is the first thing you read. That is right for a game whose score is painted area.
- The mannequin painters keep the original box-head and flat-cap identity and stay readable as a team-colour smock and cap at 120 px.
- Team-colour regions are cleanly separable for runtime tinting.

Weaknesses:
- At real in-game scale the characters are thin: limbs are single strokes. In a 4-way split they read mostly as a coloured torso with a cap, and pose detail is lost.
- The world is deliberately quiet, so the scene can feel sparse and "unfinished blueprint". There is no workshop flavour (props, tools) and no strong sense of place beyond "a drawing". A level artist would need rules for adding interest without clutter.
- The halo is functional but slightly sticker-like.
- The sprayer stream reads more as an arc of beads than a pressurised jet.
- The roller in the gameplay scene is small and seen end-on, so it reads more as a wheel than a roller. The sheet's large three-quarter roller explains it, but in play it may need a wider drum.
- The annotations (datums, dimension numbers) are lovely on a still frame but could feel like noise in motion. They should probably be fewer per screen.
comps: Splatoon (for the paint and score mechanic, not the art)
Inked: A Tale of Love (pen-on-paper world)
Bridge Constructor / Poly Bridge (blueprint and engineering framing)
Stick Fight: The Game (thin-limbed figures in a brawler)
styles.anim: Animation is cheap. The mannequins are a cutout rig: a box head, a cap, a torso slab and single-stroke limbs that pivot on the white joint circles. Pivot points are already drawn as part of the style, so skeletal or cutout animation in a 2D engine fits naturally. A light 2-3 frame line boil on the graphite outlines would sell the hand-drafted feel at almost no cost, and it is optional. The weak spot is the limbs. They are single strokes, so poses lose readability at quarter-pane size, and a jump looks almost the same as a run. Silhouettes need exaggerated poses: wide stances, big arm swings, and a squash on landing. Paint drips could be short flipbook sprites or a shader scroll on the coverage mask.
styles.engine: The style fits well. Team regions are isolated flat fills (smock, cap, sprayer reservoir, roller nap) over graphite and paper neutrals, which is exactly what grayscale-mask tinting at draw time needs. Characters can be stored as greyscale sprites with one tint mask. The world is static and can be baked as tiled paper and grid textures plus per-level hatched slab sprites; dimension and datum annotations become decals. Runtime surface paint needs the most work. The concept's glossy, dripping lip-and-spill look should become a coverage mask rendered with a small shader: a normal or bump map from the blurred mask, one specular highlight, and drip sprites stamped at mask edges. Without that shader, flat paint over hatching still reads, but it loses the 'wet spill on the drawing' quality that is the whole point. Optional shaders: a paper-grain multiply overlay, plus a faint pencil-grain mask on outlines. The live SVG filters (turbulence and specular) must not be shipped as they are.
strengths: A genuinely ownable visual grammar. Section hatching, concrete aggregate fill, datum triangles, dimension strings and a title block give a level vocabulary nobody else in the paint or platformer space uses.
Painted and unpainted surfaces cannot be confused. Paint is the only saturated, glossy, wet material on a neutral graphite world, which suits a game scored on painted area.
It keeps the author's MS-Paint identity (box head, dot eyes, flat cap, stick limbs) and upgrades it, rather than replacing it with generic art.
It is cheap and forgiving for a solo non-artist. The world is lines and patterns, roughness reads as intentional drafting, and new levels need geometry plus decals, not painting skill.
Team regions are already separated cleanly for runtime tinting.
At 480x270, paint coverage is the first thing you read, and both teams' territory is obvious.
risks: The blue/yellow pair is untested and is the weak case. Saturated yellow on warm off-white paper with beige concrete will have poor luminance contrast. It needs a dark outline or drop shadow on paint, or the paper must cool slightly. The pink/green swatch on the sheet is too small to prove that pair either.

The scene is sparse. Most of the frame is empty paper, so it can read as an unfinished prototype or 'programmer art with a concept' rather than a deliberate style, especially in screenshots and store art.

Characters are thin at quarter-pane size. In the small render they shrink to a coloured torso plus a cap, and pose, facing and weapon are hard to read. They need thicker limbs or bigger heads at real game scale.
The platforms are faint graphite. At quarter scale the unpainted slabs and ramp are low-contrast against the paper, so level geometry (where can I stand?) is harder to read than the paint.
The annotations will turn into noise in motion if they are overused. Dimension numbers that do not match the real geometry will bother the very players who like the conceit.
The roller reads as a wheel or unicycle in the side view. It needs a wider drum seen in three-quarter view, or a clearer silhouette.
The sprayer stream reads as beads rather than a jet.
The gloss and drip look depends on a custom paint shader. Without it the paint reads as flat stickers and the style loses half its charm.
styles.verdict: This is the most ownable direction for ColourWars I can see. It extends the author's crude box-head identity instead of abandoning it, and its drafting-sheet grammar has almost no direct competitor, unlike 16-bit pixel art. The execution is solid but thin. The scene is too empty, the geometry and limbs are too faint at quarter-pane size, and the blue/yellow pair on warm paper is an unaddressed contrast risk. All of these are fixable tuning issues, not flaws in the style. For a solo developer the cost-to-identity ratio is excellent, provided the runtime gloss-paint shader is treated as the one piece of real technical art the style depends on.

identity.reason: It has a very ownable grammar. The title block reads 'COLOURWARS ... DRAWN M.H.', and the mannequin painters keep the box head and cap. The glossy paint on graphite is lovely. In the render, though, the walkable geometry is faint, and the dimension text will read as UI noise. Without the gloss shader it goes flat.

production.reason: The world vocabulary is cheap (lines, hatching, decals) and forgiving. But the platforms go faint at quarter pane, the scene reads empty, and the wet-gloss paint relies on a custom shader.

player.reason: The paint reads, but the faint graphite platforms nearly vanish at quarter size, so 'where can I stand' is unclear. Sparse and pale as a capsule.

styles.name: Mid-century Geometric
styles.brief: Saul Bass / Charley Harper / mid-century poster style: characters built from primitive shapes (circle head, trapezoid body, stick limbs), flat colour fields with subtle print texture, limited muted base palette (cream, charcoal, olive, rust) so team paint pops. Strong graphic silhouettes, negative space.
styles.one_liner: A screen-printed 1950s poster that started moving: charcoal-headed painters made of a circle, a trapezoid smock and stick limbs dash across slanted charcoal slabs on warm cream paper, and the blue and orange paint is the only loud ink on the page.
styles.ownable: The painter is the original MS-Paint stick figure carried straight into Saul Bass / Charley Harper shape language, not swapped out for a new design. The flat cap with its brim is still there, now a half-disc and a slab. The dot eyes became one cream Harper eye with a pupil, set in a solid charcoal circle head. The rectangle body became an A-line smock, and the single-line limbs are kept as thick round-capped sticks. A rust-handled brush in a bib pocket marks every figure as a painter. The world uses four muted inks (cream, charcoal, olive, warm grey, plus a trace of rust), so any of the random team pairs (blue/orange, pink/green, blue/yellow) is the only saturated colour in frame. A few motifs belong to this game and nothing else: platforms cut as slanted trapezoids, painted tops drawn as a flat band with scalloped bumps and round-ended drips, the pressure sprayer's round glass reservoir showing the team's paint level, and a pale backdrop of sawtooth factory roofs, a Calder mobile, a giant paint tin and a giant brush crossing a sun disc. Players have no obvious comparison for it the way they do with pixel art. It reads as poster design or mid-century animation, not as another indie platformer.
styles.self: What works: it is clearly not pixel art and not generic flat vector. The cream-paper and limited-ink look is coherent, and the characters still carry the original game's identity (flat cap, dot eye, stick limbs, box-ish body). In the 480x270 split-screen test both players and all the paint still stand out clearly, because the backdrop stays in a narrow band of tans. The painted versus unpainted tops read at once: a grey lip against a coloured band with drips. The sprayer arc and the roller trail say what each weapon does. Weaknesses: the composition is sparse, and at full size it can look under-dressed or placeholder-like to someone not reading it as poster negative space. A real level would want more mid-century set dressing on the platform faces. At true in-game scale the characters are small and the face detail mostly disappears; they read as cap, smock and sticks, which is fine for gameplay but loses charm. The charcoal ground band is heavy and the dropout speckle on it reads a little like asphalt. The roller drum is an oblique-view cylinder, which is a compromise in a strictly side-on world. Rust and olive are near enough to orange and green that they must stay muted and out of gameplay surfaces. On the sheet, the jump pose's ground shadow is hidden behind the baseline, and the sprayer is not shown held at large scale.
comps: Agent A: A Puzzle in Disguise
Fallout's Vault Boy / atomic-age poster art
Catch Me If You Can / Saul Bass title sequences (non-game)
styles.anim: This is a natural fit for cutout or skeletal animation. The painter is a circle head, a trapezoid smock and thick round-capped stick limbs built from joints, so rigging it in Spine, DragonBones or a home-grown bone system is trivial, and a pose library (idle, run, spray, jump, roll) is cheap. Stick limbs hide the usual cutout joint seams. Snappy limited-animation timing (UPA-style holds, few in-betweens) suits the style and saves frames. Frame-by-frame is unnecessary. The print wobble must stay temporally stable, or have a deliberate slow boil at 6-8 fps, or it will shimmer. Weapons are rigid props parented to the hand. Paint drips could take a small procedural sag animation.
styles.engine: The fit is very good. Team colour sits in exactly two flat shapes (cap and smock) plus the reservoir and roller fills, so a single grayscale mask channel tints cleanly at draw time. The sheet already shows pink/green and blue/yellow working. Paint is flat bands, scallops and round-ended drips, which a runtime surface painter can generate procedurally from coverage data without texture work. Shader needs are modest but real: a screen-space paper grain/fibre overlay (multiply), a fixed dropout mask, and optionally a small stable UV-displacement wobble. Halftone on the platform faces can be baked into the tiles. Do NOT apply the print filter per sprite as the SVG does. It has to be one post pass, or the textures will swim relative to each other in a scrolling camera.
strengths: It is the strongest continuity with the author's original art: the MS-Paint stick figure and flat cap survive, translated into Bass/Harper shape language rather than replaced.
Team paint is the only saturated ink in frame, so the score (painted surface) is the most legible thing on screen, even at 480x270.
The painted vs unpainted platform tops read instantly: a grey lip against a coloured band with drips.
It is cheap for a solo non-artist: primitives, flat fills and one post-process texture. Assets are authorable in any vector tool and maintainable by script.
Weapons explain themselves: the sprayer arc, the roller trail, and the reservoir showing the paint level.
Low comparison exposure. Nobody will line it up against Celeste or Dead Cells. It reads as poster design rather than as 'another indie platformer'.
Mobile, sun disc, giant tin and brush backdrop motifs give the game its own world without adding noise.
risks: Sparse composition can read as unfinished or placeholder rather than as intentional negative space. Execution needs real set dressing (platform-face motifs, varied silhouettes) to sell 'poster' over 'prototype'.
At true in-game size the face detail (Harper eye, brush pocket) disappears. Characters become cap + smock + sticks, which is readable but loses the charm that carries the identity.
The charcoal ground and platform slabs with dropout speckle read as asphalt or granite, heavy and a little dreary, and they occupy a large share of the frame.
Muted olive (platform undersides, pedestal) sits near green team paint, and rust sits near orange. They must stay out of gameplay surfaces, or the pink/green pair will muddy.
Against cream paper a yellow team smock has weak contrast. The blue/yellow pair needs an outline or a charcoal rim on characters.
A per-asset print filter in the concept will shimmer or swim if naively ported. It has to become a stable screen-space pass.
The roller drum's oblique cylinder breaks the strict side-on flatness, and other props may tempt similar perspective cheats.
The style lives or dies on graphic-design taste (layout, rhythm, palette discipline). Poorly composed levels will look amateur faster than in pixel art.
styles.verdict: This is the most ownable direction for this author. It keeps the crude flat-cap stick figure that gives ColourWars its identity, makes paint the only loud colour on screen, and costs a solo developer far less than 16-bit pixel art while inviting almost no direct comparisons. The execution is a solid 7: readable, coherent and correctly separable for runtime tinting, but sparse and slab-heavy enough to look like a placeholder at full size. The style's potential is higher than this concept shows, provided levels get proper mid-century set dressing and the print texture becomes one stable screen-space pass.

identity.reason: It is the most polished, poster-grade still in the batch and has low comparison exposure. But the figure has drifted to a circle head with a Harper eye, so it is 'inspired by' his painter rather than his painter. The charcoal slabs are heavy, and the style depends on graphic-design taste the author may not have.

production.reason: Silhouettes read strongly at quarter pane: the chunky smock and cap figures are more legible than any stick figure here. Primitives and cutout rigging are trivial, and paint bands can be generated. The catch is that it relies on layout and palette taste more than the crude styles do. It needs one stable post pass, and badly composed levels will look amateur fast.

player.reason: Charcoal slabs carry the paint well, and the figures have clear shape language with filled smocks, so they read better than stick figures. It reads as tasteful poster art but a little dreary and sparse. Olive and rust sit too close to green and orange.

styles.name: Construction-Paper Collage
styles.brief: Everything is cut and torn construction paper / card: torn fibrous edges, drop shadows showing layered depth, bits of masking tape, scissor-cut characters with split-pin joints. Team paint is wet poster paint on top of the paper (glossy, drips).
styles.one_liner: Box-headed paper-doll painters, cut with scissors and jointed with brass split pins, splash glossy wet poster paint across torn-card platforms taped to a muted sugar-paper workshop.
styles.ownable: It keeps the original MS-Paint identity rather than replacing it. The painter is still the box head with two dot eyes, a flat-line mouth, a flat cap with a brim and a rectangular body. Now those shapes are cut from card, and the limbs are card strips that rotate on visible brass split pins. That reads as cut-out animation (South Park, Terry Gilliam, a school-craft table), and few platformers have it, so players have no ready pixel-art comparison. The material contrast does the gameplay work. The world is matte, fibrous and muted: torn edges with a white paper core, masking tape and soft layered drop shadows. Team paint is the only glossy thing on screen: specular, wet, sitting proud of the card and dripping over each platform's front lip. So "what is painted" (the score) is also "what is shiny". Team colour sits only on the cap, the overalls, the sprayer's paint jar and the roller sleeve, which are flat single-colour regions that can be tinted at runtime. The rig is also exactly what a cutout skeleton animates, so the medium and the production method match.
styles.self:
What works: the medium is clear at a glance (torn rims, tape, layered shadows, brass pins). Paint is clearly the most saturated and only glossy element, so coverage reads as the score even at 480x270. The background stays low-contrast and out of the way, and the box-head painter carries the original game's identity into a craft medium. The weak points:

- **Players at quarter size:** at the honest ~110 px scale they read in the 480x270 render mostly through their team-colour cap and overalls plus the cream rim; the face and pins disappear. A wider body or a bigger cap might be needed in 4-player split.
- **Roller pose:** the roller painter's pose is a bit stiff and hunched; the drum reads, but the pushing gesture is not fully convincing.
- **Backdrop:** it is pleasant but generic (factory roofline, clouds, sun, newsprint scraps) and could carry more painter-workshop personality without competing.
- **Paint surface:** the paint is uniformly glossy, so roller trail and spray splatter only differ by shape; a real spec should give them different textures.
- **Gameplay ambiguity:** platforms look like they float, held only by tape, with no support, which may raise "can I stand under this?" questions.
- **Fonts:** sheet labels depend on Segoe Print being installed.

Files are in the session scratchpad, concepts/collage/: scene.svg (~176 KB), character.svg (~82 KB), and the matching scene.png, scene_small.png and character.png.
comps: Paper Mario (esp. The Origami King / Color Splash, which is literally paint on paper)
South Park: The Stick of Truth / The Fractured But Whole (cutout rig)
Gang Beasts / Human Fall Flat (box-ish ragdoll figures, loosely)
styles.anim: This is a pure cutout rig: about 10 rigid card pieces pivoting on visible split pins, with no in-betweens to draw. You can animate it in Spine or DragonBones, or with in-engine bone transforms. A bit of stepped timing (animating on 2s or 3s) would make it feel deliberately craft-like and hide stiff curves, so a non-animator can get there. The pins also explain why the joints are rigid, so weak arcs read as style rather than as a mistake. The roller push pose is the weak link and needs IK, or a hand-tuned arm chain, to keep the drum on the floor. That is a moderate cost. Paint drips, splats and flecks are small spawned sprites. Optional extra: a subtle 2-frame jitter on the paper texture or shadow offset to suggest stop-motion, which is cheap.
styles.engine: The engine tints greyscale masks at draw time, and that fits the team regions well: the cap, the overalls, the sprayer's jar and the roller sleeve are flat single-colour shapes. Author them as greyscale card with the grain baked in, then multiply-tint. The world fits sprites well too: backdrop layers, tape and props are static sprites. Platforms need care, because levels have arbitrary widths. Use a 9-slice or 3-slice card strip with torn-edge caps and a tiling torn top edge, or the torn edges will repeat or stretch visibly. Runtime surface paint is where the shader work is. The 'only glossy thing' promise needs a pass that turns the painted-coverage mask into a blurred height field, then into a normal or specular highlight (one cheap fullscreen or per-surface pass), plus drip sprites spawned along platform lips as coverage crosses them. Without that shader the paint is flat colour and loses half its identity. A fullscreen paper-grain multiply overlay (one tiling texture) is optional but cheap, and it unifies everything. Drop shadows can be baked into the sprites or done as one offset darkened draw. None of this is exotic, but the gloss-from-mask shader is a real must-have.
strengths: It keeps the author's box-head, flat-cap, dot-eye identity and gives it a material, so the style feels like an evolution of the original rather than a replacement. That is the strongest argument for this route over generic 16-bit pixel art.
The matte-world vs glossy-paint contrast is a smart gameplay rule: 'shiny = scored' is a legible, ownable visual language. Paint is clearly the most saturated element in the full-size scene.

Rendering paint only along platform top edges, with drips over the lip as decoration, matches score = surface coverage and stays readable. The contested blue/orange seam on the character sheet reads well.
Cutout rigs on split pins are about the cheapest credible animation method for a non-artist, and roughness reads as craft rather than incompetence (forgiving bar).
The muted sugar-paper backdrop really does recede and leaves value room for any team pair.
Production assets can come from real scanned card and tape plus a phone camera, which is realistic for a solo developer and makes the style hard to clone convincingly.
risks: At the quarter-pane size (480x270) the characters are about 30 px tall. The collage medium mostly vanishes there: torn rims, tape, pins and gloss all fall below resolution, and the scene reads as a muted flat-vector platformer. The style's identity only shows at full-screen or 2-player sizes.

A player standing on their own team's paint loses figure-ground contrast. The blue painter on the blue floor strip, and the orange one next to orange paint, nearly merge in the small render. The cream die-cut rim is too thin to save it at 4-player size. It needs a thicker outline, a bigger head and cap, or a darker overall value for the body.

The yellow and green pairs are untested in the scene. Yellow wet paint on the cream or sugar-paper backdrop and its tan props will have weak value contrast wherever paint spills off the grey platforms or sits near background-coloured elements.

Execution is procedural-looking. The feTurbulence grain and jittered tears read as an 'SVG filter demo' more than real paper, so the concept undersells the style. A real version depends on scanned materials, which the concept does not prove.
The 2-player scene is sparse: large empty mid-ground and small figures. It is hard to judge how dense, busy paint (many splats, mid-air projectiles) will look against the low-contrast world.
Taped platforms floating on nothing raise collision and solidity questions (can I stand under, jump through?). The grey slate platforms also read a bit like generic UI bars rather than card.

Comparison exposure: anyone who has played Paper Mario: Color Splash (painting a paper world) or Tearaway or LittleBigPlanet will make the link immediately, though the box-head dolls are distinct enough to avoid looking derivative.
Gloss lives or dies by a runtime shader on the coverage mask. If that is cut, the paint becomes flat colour and the core matte-vs-glossy idea collapses.
The idle pose has an odd arm crossing the torso, and the roller pose is stiff. These are minor, but they show the rig needs care to avoid looking like a clip-art puppet.
styles.verdict: This style has real potential for this author: it keeps the crude box-head identity, gives it a material reason to look simple, and its matte-world vs glossy-paint rule maps directly onto the score. This execution undersells it. The procedural textures look like SVG filters rather than paper, the scene is sparse, and at 4-player quarter-pane size the craft details and gloss disappear, while players merge into their own team's paint. It is worth pursuing over generic pixel art, but only if the next pass proves split-screen legibility first: bigger heads and caps, a thicker die-cut outline, all three colour pairs tested, and gloss that survives downscaling.

identity.reason: The medium mostly vanishes at quarter-pane size, players merge into their own team's paint, and it sits next to Paper Mario Color Splash, which is literally painting a paper world.

production.reason: The cutout rig is cheap, but the medium disappears at quarter pane, players merge into their own team's paint, and real scanned materials plus a gloss shader are required.

player.reason: Players merge into their own team's paint at quarter size. The craft detail vanishes, and it reads as a muted flat-vector platformer with a strong Paper Mario comparison.

styles.name: Sidewalk Chalk
styles.brief: Chalk drawn on asphalt or a dark slate board: dusty chalk strokes, smudges, pastel-ish chalk colours for the world, characters as chalk drawings. Team paint is thick wet paint that contrasts with the dry dusty chalk (different material = readable score).
styles.one_liner: The original MS-Paint box-head painter redrawn in dusty sidewalk chalk on dark tarmac, with team colour as thick, glossy, dripping wet paint lying on top of the dry pastel-chalk platforms.
styles.ownable: The concept is built on a contrast between two materials, and that contrast doubles as the scoring rule: the world is dry, grainy pastel chalk, and anything that scores is wet, shiny paint with drips and a cast shadow. A player can tell what is painted from how it looks, before colour comes into it. The characters are the author's own original figure, kept as it was: box head, two dot eyes, a flat mouth, a flat cap, a rectangular body and single-line limbs. It is now drawn in white chalk, and the cap and overalls are filled with team paint. That keeps the identity that was 'weird and basic' and gives it a reason to look that way, because chalk stick figures are what people actually draw on pavements. The backdrop is a pavement with expansion joints, aggregate speckle and half-washed ghosts of old chalk drawings (sun, clouds, hopscotch, heart, star, palm-wipe smears). No pixel-art or vector-platformer reference sits ready for comparison. Team re-tinting is simple: the cap, overalls, sprayer jar and roller sleeve are the only paint regions on the character, and everything else is fixed white chalk.
styles.self: Strengths: the two-material idea works. In the 480x270 quarter-pane test both players and every painted surface stand out clearly from the grey-violet chalk and dark tarmac, and the gloss and drips say 'this is the score' without any UI. The original stick-figure identity carries over with charm, and the cap/overalls tint regions are clean and separable, as the pink and green versions show. The ghost doodles give a distinct sense of place without competing with the players. Weaknesses: the chalk fill texture on platforms is close to noise at 1:1 and reads more like 'textured carpet' than individual chalk strokes up close. The floor hatching is regular enough to look a little like rain streaks. The sprayer is deliberately crude and boxy, and on the character sheet it looks more like a doodle than a desirable weapon. In-game, the 52x120 figure is small, so the face (chalk eyes on a dusty grey box) almost disappears at quarter scale and only the cap and overalls carry identity. The scene's upper-middle backdrop is quite empty. Yellow team paint on the pale lavender chalk was not tested and may be weak. The style also depends on runtime effects (grain, gloss, stroke boil), so a flat sprite export would lose much of what sells it.
styles.anim: Frame-by-frame line art suits this well. The figures are stick limbs and a box, so 4-6 frame cycles per state are cheap to draw. Stroke boil (re-jitter or swap between 2-3 drawings every ~100ms) sells the chalk look and also hides crude in-betweening, because roughness reads as intended. A cutout rig would also work: box head, rectangle body and line limbs. Paint effects (drips, splats, the arc of the jet) are procedural or particle decals, not hand animation. Overall cost is low. The most expensive part is the wet-paint edge treatment (drips growing at mask edges), which is shader or engine work, not art.
styles.engine: Fits the tint-mask approach well. Cap, overalls, sprayer jar and roller sleeve are the only tinted regions, and the rest is fixed white chalk, so a grayscale mask plus a draw-time tint maps directly. Runtime paint needs the most: to get the material contrast that carries the style, painted coverage needs a gloss pass (a normal from the blurred coverage mask plus a specular term), a drop shadow and drip decals spawned at mask edges. Flat tinted fills would lose most of the "wet vs dry" read. Chalk grain can be baked into tiling platform textures. An optional screen-space grain overlay and a slow-noise UV wobble on chalk sprites would add a lot for little cost. None of this needs per-frame SVG filters. It all reduces to textures and one or two small shaders.
strengths: The two-material idea (dry chalk world, glossy wet paint) makes the score readable from material alone, before colour comes into it. That is a real design idea, not just a look.
It keeps the author's original box-head stick figure and gives a reason for it to look that way (people draw chalk stick figures on pavements), so the crude identity becomes intentional.
At the 480x270 quarter-pane size, players and every painted strip are clearly legible. Cap and overalls carry identity even when the face disappears.
The tint regions are clean and few, and the pink/green versions on the sheet show the re-tint works.
It is forgiving to make: wobbly, imperfect strokes look on-style, which suits a non-artist solo dev using hand-drawn or tablet assets.
Few ready-made comparisons in the platform-shooter space. It reads as its own thing, not as 'another pixel-art platformer'.
risks: The ground slab is teal-green chalk. Green team paint (pink/green pair) on it is untested and will likely lose hue contrast, and the same goes for yellow paint on the pale lavender platforms. The pastel world palette needs to sit away from every team hue, or be near-neutral.

The wet gloss currently looks like glossy plastic or jelly more than paint. It is readable but slightly toy-like, and it depends entirely on a runtime shader. Ship flat tinted fills and the core idea collapses.
Platform chalk fill reads as noisy carpet texture, and the diagonal hatching on the floor and side walls looks like rain. Up close, the world has less craft than the characters.
The backdrop is a large empty dark field (the whole upper middle), and the ghost doodles are almost invisible at quarter size. Levels may feel barren unless the doodles are authored per stage.
The face is lost at gameplay scale. Emotes and hit reactions will have to come from pose and cap, not expression.
The sprayer design is weak, more doodle than desirable weapon. Weapon variety and readability of weapon silhouettes will need more care than the character.
Dark tarmac with bright paint is high contrast, but in 4-pane split screen the dark world plus pane dividers may feel heavy and gloomy without lighting variety.
styles.verdict: The style itself is strong, and the strongest thing about it is the design idea: dry chalk against wet paint makes the score readable without UI, and it turns the author's crude box-head figure into an intentional, ownable look with few direct competitors. This concept carries it out competently but not finished. Paint and characters read well at quarter-pane size, but the platform texture is noisy, the floor hatching looks like rain, the backdrop is empty, the gloss looks like plastic, and the teal floor and lavender platforms would clash with green and yellow teams. All of those can be fixed with palette and texture choices and need no change of direction. That gives it a much lower bar and much lower comparison exposure than 16-bit pixel art.

identity.reason: The dry-chalk-versus-wet-paint material rule is a real idea, and pavement stick figures justify the crude figure. But the gloss looks like plastic jelly, the teal floor and lavender platforms will clash with the green and yellow teams, and the hatching reads as rain.

production.reason: Very readable on dark tarmac and forgiving to draw. But the platform fill and floor hatching are noisy, the teal and lavender world palette fights the green and yellow teams, and the core wet-versus-dry read depends on a gloss shader.

player.reason: The dark slate makes both players and all the glossy paint pop. Wet paint against dry chalk is a good readability rule. The teal floor and lavender platforms will clash with green and yellow teams, and the platform texture is noisy.

styles.name: Stained Glass
styles.brief: The arena is a stained-glass window: thick dark lead came lines dividing every surface into cells; uncoloured cells are clear/frosted pale glass; painted surfaces become glowing coloured glass in team colour. Characters are lead-lined glass figures too. Light glows through the glass.
styles.one_liner: A cathedral window made of clear, colourless glass that painters fill in with glowing team colour as they play. The original box-headed stick painter is rebuilt in lead and glass, so his single-line limbs are now strips of lead came.
styles.ownable: The medium and the mechanic are the same idea. Every walkable surface starts as clear frosted glass, and painting it turns it into glowing coloured glass. "Painting the arena" becomes "staining the window", and the end-of-match reveal can be read as the window being finished. The rest of the world is grisaille: grey stone mullions, a pale diamond-quarry lattice in the lancets and smoky slate-glass platform bodies. That leaves team colour as the only saturated hue on screen, so the score is the most visible thing in every frame. The original character's identity carries across almost unchanged and gains meaning. Dot eyes and the flat mouth are literally blobs and a strip of lead. The single-line limbs become lead-edged glass strips. The box head and flat cap become panes. Players have no ready comparison for it: it is not pixel art, not vector-flat and not a hand-drawn imitation of anything. It also leaves room for a matching UI later, for example a rose-window score reveal or lead-framed panels.
styles.self:
What works: the scene reads instantly as a stained-glass arena. The backdrop is calm and stays out of the way of the players and the paint. In the 480x270 quarter-pane test, both players, the spray arc and the paint strips still separate cleanly from the world. The painter keeps the charm of the MS-Paint original: box head, dot eyes, flat cap. Team regions (cap, overalls, legs, sprayer tank and nozzle, roller drum) are cleanly separable for runtime tinting, and pink and green swaps are shown.

Weaknesses:
- The "glows with light" quality is only partly sold. The halos and bloom are subtle, and on the pale backdrop the paint looks more like bright enamel than light passing through glass. A darker or dusk version of the window, or a real emissive pass, would sell the backlighting much more.
- The platform bodies are a heavy grey and the ground slab takes up a lot of the bottom of the frame.
- At full size the paint strip, 28 px tall, reads well. In the quarter pane it is about 7 px and depends on the glow to carry it.
- At sheet scale the characters look partly like thick-outlined cartoons rather than leaded glass. More internal came cuts and stronger glass texture inside the large figures would help.
- Spray droplets are small faceted gems and lose detail in the quarter pane.
- Yellow (the third team pair) is not shown. Yellow glass on pale frosted glass will be the weakest contrast case and needs testing.

Files, all in the session scratchpad, concepts/stainedglass/: scene.svg, scene.png, scene_small.png, character.svg, character.png, and the generator gen.py. Each PNG was rendered from the final version of its SVG.
comps: Hollow Knight (stained-glass arenas such as the Watcher's Spire and Radiance windows)
Chicory: A Colorful Tale (painting a colourless world)
styles.anim: This style suits a cutout rig better than most. Every limb and panel is a lead-edged pane that moves rigidly, and thick black came hides joint seams. Frame-by-frame is not needed: a cutout or skeletal rig with 6-10 parts per character covers idle, run and jump cheaply. Do not boil the lead lines; glass should look rigid, and wobble would undercut the medium. Paint drops can be small faceted gem sprites. The one costly part is keeping pane cuts consistent across rotations, because came lines inside a rotating limb must rotate with it. Bake those cuts into the part sprites, not into the pose.
styles.engine: The world fits well. Unpainted panes are pale grey-white, so they tint cleanly from a grayscale mask. Platforms can be tile modules with lead lines baked into a fixed overlay sprite that sits above the paint layer. Runtime paint fits better than in most styles: quantise coverage to pane cells, or simply draw the lead overlay over a freeform paint mask so the came lines hide paint edges, and the medium covers a crude paint system. Characters split cleanly into tinted team regions (cap, overalls, tank, roller drum) and untinted regions (skin, grey metal, lead). The style's main selling point does need shaders, though. Light glowing through the glass needs an additive or emissive pass plus bloom on painted cells, and a cheap seedy-glass streak texture overlay; without them it reads as flat enamel tiles, as it does here. A refraction or normal ripple is optional. The backdrop should be one static parallax sprite.
strengths: Medium and mechanic are the same idea: unpainted means clear glass, painted means stained glass, and the finished match is a finished window. This is a strong, ownable pitch with almost no ready comparison in paint shooters.
The grisaille world leaves team colour as the only saturated hue, so blue/orange coverage strips pop even at quarter size.
The original box-head, dot-eye, flat-cap character survives almost intact. The thick lead outline is a natural upgrade of the MS-Paint line, not a replacement.
Thick dark came lines are forgiving: they hide rough edges, paint-mask seams and simple rigging, and they keep silhouettes legible in split-screen.
The procedural approach (pane splitting, lead overlay) is authorable by a non-artist and can be generated by script, as gen.py shows.
It naturally suggests a matching UI later, such as a rose-window score reveal and lead-framed panels, which fits the user's plan to fix gameplay first and then the UI.
risks: The concept's central promise, light glowing through glass, is not delivered. On a pale, washed-out backdrop the paint reads as bright bathroom tiles or enamel, not lit glass. The backdrop probably needs to be darker (dusk or night nave) for the style to work at all, and that is a palette rethink, not a tweak.

The characters read as thick-outlined cartoon figures (close to a Flash-game look), not leaded glass. Remove the glass framing and they could belong to any style, so the medium gets diluted on the most-watched objects.

The paintable surface is a thin 28 px strip on top of a heavy grey slab, so most of each platform is unpaintable grey. That weakens 'score is painted surface' visually, and the strip is about 7 px in the quarter pane.
Yellow on pale frosted glass is the obvious weak pair and is untested. White frosted unpainted panes also sit close to the white backdrop, so contested areas are muddy.
