Glow, bloom and glass texture depend on shaders. Without them, the shipped game looks like the flat version here.
The ground slab and stone backdrop are busy grey-on-grey noise that competes with no one but adds visual weight without adding information.
styles.verdict: The idea is one of the more ownable directions available. Staining a colourless window as the score is a real conceit, it keeps the author's box-head painter almost intact, and nothing in the paint-shooter field looks like it. This execution falls short: on a bright, washed-out backdrop the painted panes read as flat enamel tiles, and the thick-outlined characters read as cartoons, so the glowing-glass promise is not delivered. Before it can be judged fairly against the pixel-art candidate, it needs one more pass with a dark nave backdrop, emissive and bloom on painted cells, and a taller paint band.

identity.reason: The conceit (stain the window as you score) is strong, but the execution reads as enamel tiles and thick-outlined cartoons. It needs a palette rethink and bloom shaders before it can even be judged.

production.reason: The core promise, light through glass, needs emissive and bloom passes plus a darker palette rethink. As shown it reads as enamel tiles, and it is not forgiving.

player.reason: The glow is not delivered. Paint is a 7 px enamel strip on heavy grey slabs, frosted white glass sits next to a white backdrop, and the style would need a full palette rethink.

styles.name: Pop-Art Comic
styles.brief: Lichtenstein / Roy-era comic print: heavy black outlines, Ben-Day dot fills, flat primaries, speed lines, onomatopoeia bursts (SPLAT!). Characters are bold cartoon painters. Team paint as solid flat fills with dot shading.
styles.one_liner: The original MS-Paint box-head painter, inked like a 1963 comic panel: chunky black outlines, Ben-Day dots on the skin and in the shading, flat primary team paint that drips off halftone-grey slabs, with SPLAT! bursts and speed lines over a quiet newsprint workshop.
styles.ownable: It keeps the author's own figure and builds the style around it. The box head, two dot eyes, flat-line mouth, brimmed cap, rectangular body and single-line limbs all stay; the limbs are now heavy ink strokes, so it is still a stick figure. Lichtenstein-style red-dot skin and a slight print misregistration make it read as a printed comic rather than vector art. Not many games have taken the Roy Lichtenstein / Ben-Day print look, and I can't think of a 2D paint shooter that has, so players won't have an obvious game to compare it to the way they do with pixel art. The look also fits how the game scores. All terrain is neutral halftone grey and is never a team hue, so the only flat saturated colour on screen is team paint, and the score reads straight off the image. Onomatopoeia (SPLAT!, SKRRRSH, FSSSH!) is one place a sound-effect system could build its own identity.
styles.self:
**What came out well:**
- The characters are appealing and clearly come from the author's original stick figure: the box head, dot eyes, flat mouth and cap read well even at 120 px.
- Team identity is unmistakable.
- Paint coverage, at roughly 50% of walkable surfaces, pops strongly against the grey halftone terrain.
- At 480x270, players, paint and the SPLAT burst are all readable, and the backdrop stays quiet.
- The sheet's comic-page panel layout, yellow caption boxes and FSSSH!/SPLAT! lettering sell the medium.

**Weaknesses:**
- The scene backdrop (arched windows, wainscot, lamps in thin tan line) is restrained to the point of being slightly bland. It reads more "clean comic" than full Lichtenstein. A bolder treatment, like large flat dot areas or heavier ink, would push the style but risks competing with the players.
- At gameplay scale the Ben-Day dots on skin and paint are tiny and mostly disappear, so in play the style leans on outlines plus SFX lettering. Dots would need to be screen-space and larger in production.
- The SPLAT! burst is the brightest element in the frame. Frequent bursts in a four-player match could get noisy and would need rate limiting.
- The roller handle passes over the drum somewhat crudely.
- Speed lines overlap the SKRRRSH lettering a little.
- Every hue clashes with some team pair, so the world palette is limited to cream, grey and black. That is safe but limits how colourful the environment can be.
comps: Splatoon (the paint-shooter genre comparison regardless of style)
Hi-Fi Rush (comic onomatopoeia and halftone accents)
Marvel's Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (film, Ben-Day / misregistration look)
styles.anim: The characters are a box torso and head with constant-width ink-stroke limbs, so they suit a cutout rig: rigid head, torso and cap parts plus procedurally drawn limb strokes, or a few hand-keyed poses (idle, run, jump, fire, roll) at 6 to 12 fps, which is what comics imply anyway. Low frame counts look intentional here rather than cheap. Line boil (2 to 3 alternate inks swapped at about 8 fps) would add print-life cheaply, but it would fight a stable screen-space Ben-Day shader, so pick one. Burst and SFX lettering are just sprite pops with a scale-overshoot tween. Paint drips can be procedural along the coverage edge. Overall this is one of the cheaper styles to animate convincingly.
styles.engine: Good fit, with one shader dependency. Team colour sits in clean, separable regions (cap, overalls, tank, drum), so grayscale-mask tinting at draw time works directly: ink, mask and skin are three layers. Runtime-painted surfaces are a flat-fill band with an ink edge, and drips can be generated from the coverage mask. The style's main signature, Ben-Day dots, has to come from a screen-space halftone shader (dot size fixed at any camera zoom, driven by a shade or luminance channel). Baked into sprites, the dots alias and disappear at quarter-pane size, which the 480x270 render already shows. Misregistration is a cheap per-layer UV offset, and paper grain is a full-screen overlay. That is two or three small post or material shaders, all routine.
strengths: Keeps the author's own box-head, cap and stick-limb figure and gives it a polished look without losing its oddness. This is the strongest argument against generic pixel art.
Score readability is built into the palette: terrain is neutral halftone grey or cream and never a team hue, so flat saturated paint is the only loud colour on screen.
Forgiving execution bar. Thick outlines, flat fills and limited poses look intentional, which suits a non-artist solo developer.
Few direct game comparisons for a 2D paint shooter. Comix Zone and Viewtiful Joe are old and in other genres, so players have no obvious game to measure it against.
The white sticker halo separates players from the busy terrain well at 480x270.
SFX lettering (SPLAT!, SKRRRSH, FSSSH!) gives the game its own feedback vocabulary that ties visuals and audio together.
Assets are vector-like and parametric. AI concepts can be redrawn as clean ink, mask and halftone layers, and that is maintainable.
risks: The Ben-Day dots, the defining pop-art feature, vanish at gameplay and quarter-pane scale. Without a screen-space halftone shader it reads as clean flat cartoon, not Lichtenstein.

The cream backdrop is a problem for the blue/yellow pair. Yellow paint on a cream wall and tan trim will have noticeably weaker contrast than blue/orange, and the pale blue backdrop dots tint toward the blue team. This palette was only shown with blue/orange in the scene.

The backdrop is underdesigned: thin tan line art, empty and generic. It reads as clip-art more than a confident comic panel, so a full game needs a stronger environment language that still stays quiet.

SPLAT! bursts are the highest-contrast element in the frame. Four players firing constantly will turn the screen into lettering noise unless bursts are rate-limited and reserved for meaningful events (big hits, splats, KOs).
Characters are small in the 1600x900 frame (about 120 px). Weapons such as the roller handle read crudely, and the sprayer stream is thin at quarter size.
Painted bands with drips and glints add visual noise along every surface edge at high coverage, which could make platform edges harder to read for collision.
Grey terrain plus cream walls makes every level look alike. Variety has to come from silhouettes and props, because the palette is locked.
styles.verdict: The style suits this game well: it keeps the author's own figure, makes paint the only saturated colour on screen, and is forgiving enough for a non-artist to carry. The concept's execution is only decent. The backdrop is bland, the dots that make the look are lost at gameplay scale, and yellow-on-cream contrast was never tested. Choose it over 16-bit pixel art for identity, but only with a screen-space halftone shader and a bolder environment pass. Without those it collapses into generic clean vector cartoon.

identity.reason: It keeps the figure with a thick outline. But the Ben-Day dots, which define the style, vanish at gameplay scale, leaving generic clean cartoon art, and SPLAT bursts will turn into noise with four players.

production.reason: Forgiving with thick outlines, but its signature Ben-Day dots need a screen-space halftone shader, and the SPLAT lettering becomes noise with four players.

player.reason: Highest first-impression energy for a trailer: thick outlines, SPLAT bursts, and figures that read clearly with a white halo. Paint reads, but grey terrain plus a cream wall is busy, the lettering becomes noise with four players firing, and yellow on cream is risky.

styles.name: Linocut Print
styles.brief: Hand-carved linocut / woodblock print: single dark ink on cream paper, visible gouge marks carved into flat areas, chunky slightly uneven shapes, ink texture where coverage is imperfect. Team paint as a second hand-printed colour pass.
styles.one_liner: A two-pass linocut print: chunky warm-black carved slabs with gouge marks and wood grain on cream paper over a pale tint-block factory skyline, with team paint laid on top as a slightly misregistered second colour pass of blue and orange.
styles.ownable: It is a printmaking language, not a pixel or vector-cartoon one, so players have no obvious game to compare it with. The original MS-Paint painter survives almost unchanged: a box head left as cream paper with an ink keyline, square dot eyes, a flat-line mouth, a flat cap with a brim, a rectangular body, and stubby stroke limbs. Carving it in lino gives it craft without losing its odd charm. The medium also suits the game's rule. The world is the ink block, the score is the colour pass printed on top, so painted ground and unpainted ground are as different as an inked block and a coloured one. The small misregistration between the ink and colour layers is a signature detail that also keeps the team-colour regions (cap, overalls, sprayer tank, roller drum, floor paint) cleanly separable for runtime tinting. Supporting motifs: chained hanging timber platforms, brick-coursed floors with corner shading gouges, carved sky swoops and a ringed sun, all in one limited palette.
styles.self:
What came out well: the medium reads straight away, through solid ink slabs, carved highlight lines, brick and grain gouges, the patchy ink-starved grain and the colour pass sitting on top. The players and paint stand out clearly at 480x270. Blue and orange bands are the brightest things in the frame, and the cream-faced painters with team caps and overalls are recognisable even at quarter size. The background tint block stays quiet. The cream face with ink dots ties the design straight back to the author's original stick figures. The surface swatches (bare, contested, claimed) make the score read cleanly.

Weak points:
- At 1:1 game scale the faces and overall straps are only a few pixels, so the charm lives mostly in the silhouette and cap.
- The character poses are stiff, and the front arm crossing the torso reads a bit like a strap.
- The procedural gouges are more regular than a real hand-carved block; a human carver would give much richer, form-following cut patterns, especially in the sky and on the figures.
- The ink-starved grain patches on the ground are slightly heavy and could look like dirt or noise in motion.
- The two smoke curls are a little cartoonish against the otherwise flat print.
- The spray stream is a good arc of droplets but has less carved 'motion line' character than a printmaker would give it.
- The pink and green pair work, but pure #00FF00 sits uneasily against the warm paper. Colour passes might want slightly print-ink-adjusted values with the tint applied over a mask.
comps: Pentiment (woodcut and print-shop passages, the closest printmaking-language game)
Limbo (dark platform silhouettes over a pale sky)
Inkulinati (paper and ink as the game world)
Return of the Obra Dinn (limited-ink print look, a looser comparison)
styles.anim: Animate frame by frame at a low rate (8-12 fps), with a few chunky poses for idle, run, jump and fire. Low frame rates look natural in a print style, so few frames are needed. Line boil can be faked by cycling two or three fixed grain or edge variants of each frame, which is cheap and suits the medium. Shimmering per-frame procedural noise would read as static, so avoid it. Cutout rigs are possible because the body is boxy, but they would expose clean vector edges unless every part keeps its carved edge. Each frame needs two layers: an ink layer and a greyscale team mask. That roughly doubles authoring per frame but is mechanical work. The current poses are stiff, and the arms read as blobs and straps, so motion design needs real work. The medium does not provide it.
styles.engine: A strong fit. The two-pass print idea matches the engine's model directly: an ink sprite plus a greyscale team mask tinted at draw time, with a 1-2 px offset for the misregistration, which costs nothing. Runtime surface paint should be a mask-revealed overlay sampled from one tiling brayer-texture proof, so generated coverage keeps its starved, broken edge. Use a world-space texture with fixed UVs so it does not swim. Optional shaders: a full-screen paper-fibre overlay (cheap, multiply), and possibly a static per-texture edge-wobble bake rather than any live displacement. Nothing needs per-frame noise. Palette caveat: blue/yellow is the weak pair. Yellow projectiles and yellow-capped figures against the cream paper sky will lose contrast, so the yellow pass needs an ink keyline or a darker ochre adjustment. Pure #00FF00 also clashes with the warm paper, as the artist admits. All painted surfaces sit on near-black ink, so floor coverage itself reads well for every pair.
strengths: Painted versus unpainted ground is the best separation of any style direction here. Saturated colour on near-black ink slabs is unmistakable, even at the 480x270 quarter pane.
The 'world is the ink block, score is the colour pass' idea is a real conceptual hook tied to the scoring rule, not decoration.
Keeps the author's MS-Paint painter almost intact (cream box head, dot eyes, flat cap, stubby limbs). The crude charm survives and now looks intentional.
Low comparison exposure: no prominent game owns linocut print for action, and almost none in the paint-shooter genre.
A limited palette and no shading make volume production feasible for a non-artist. Roughness reads as craft, not error.
Splits cleanly into an ink layer and a tint mask for runtime team colouring. Misregistration is a free signature detail.
The quiet tint-block background stays out of the way of gameplay.
risks: As executed, it reads more as grunge or screenprint vector than linocut. Platforms are mostly flat black with faint scratches, and real lino would show many more white carved cuts that follow the form. The look depends heavily on hand-carved detail that procedural gouges don't convincingly fake.
The ink-starved speckle patches on the floor look like dirt or snow and will look like noise in motion and at small scale.
Faces and overall straps vanish at 1:1 game scale, so players are identified mainly by cap and body colour. That works for gameplay but loses the charm the author values.
Blue/yellow on cream paper: the yellow team's figures and airborne spray against the sky will be weak without a keyline or an adjusted ochre.
Characters are stiff, and the arms read as blobs or straps. Animation quality will decide whether this looks charming or crude.
Making it authentic (scanned proofs, carved stamps) is a real craft time sink. Making it cheap (filters) risks the generic 'texture overlay' look.
Dark-on-cream with large black structures could feel heavy and monotonous over a full set of levels. Level variety has to come from shape, because there is no palette to vary.
styles.verdict: The concept is right and the execution is middling. The ink-block-plus-colour-pass idea gives the best paint readability and one of the most ownable identities on offer, and it keeps the author's box-head painter. Currently it looks like grunge-filtered vector more than carved lino. Solid black platforms, sparse gouges and speckle noise lack the dense, form-following cut marks that sell the medium. As a direction it is worth pursuing over generic 16-bit pixel art, provided the next pass commits to authentic carved texture (scanned or hand-drawn cuts, fixed per asset), fixes yellow against the cream paper, and gives the figures livelier poses.

identity.reason: Paint on near-black slabs separates very well, and the 'ink block plus colour pass' idea fits the scoring rule. The figure survives as a cream box head. In the render it reads as grunge-filtered vector rather than carved lino, and the speckle on the floor looks like dirt.

production.reason: Paint on black slabs reads very well. But authenticity means hand-carved or scanned texture per asset, and procedural gouges come out looking like a grunge filter. That is a time sink for a non-artist.

player.reason: Coverage contrast is the strongest of all: saturated bands on near-black slabs are unmistakable for every pair. The small render is graphic and punchy, with chunky silhouettes and good capsule appeal. Yellow on the cream sky only affects figures and airborne spray, not the score surfaces. The speckle on the floor reads as dirt.

styles.name: Vinyl Sticker Toy
styles.brief: Characters and props are glossy die-cut vinyl stickers with thick white sticker borders and a small drop shadow, chunky designer-toy proportions (big head, small body). Environment is a sticker sheet / lunchbox / laptop-lid surface with stickers placed on it. Team paint as glossy splats.
styles.one_liner: Chunky designer-toy painters in flat caps, cut out as glossy vinyl stickers with fat white die-cut borders, slapping drippy paint-splat stickers across ruler, sticking-plaster and kraft-paper platforms stuck to a dark brushed laptop lid.
styles.ownable: The whole game is a physical object. Every gameplay thing (painter, weapon, platform, paint) is a die-cut sticker with the same white border and drop shadow. The backdrop is the surface they are stuck to, a dark brushed laptop lid with a few faded, peeling stickers left over. That gives a reading nobody gets from pixel art, a "my laptop lid became the level" toy feel, and it carries over to UI later: HUD pieces can be stickers, and score reveals can be sticker sheets or peel-offs. The painter keeps the original MS-Paint DNA (box head, two dot eyes, flat line mouth, flat cap with a brim) but rebuilt as a big-headed vinyl toy, so the author's identity survives the upgrade. Paint is itself a sticker: glossy blue or orange drips stuck on top of the platforms. Score ownership is a plain figure-ground read (saturated gloss on neutral kraft), and stickering over territory fits how players will think about it. Platforms are everyday stationery objects (a ruler, a sticking plaster, a kraft floor strip with a ramp), and that gives each level a theme hook.
styles.self: What works: the medium reads at a glance, with white die-cut borders, gloss and shadows on everything in play. Characters are readable and appealing, and they clearly descend from the original box-head stick figures. The 480x270 quarter-pane test passes. Players and paint are the brightest, most saturated elements against the dark lid, the backdrop stickers recede, and the blue vs orange territory is legible from a distance. The character sheet shows all three poses in both teams, plus pink and green, both weapons large, and bare / contested / owned surface swatches. Weaknesses: the scene is sparse. Only the floor and the two platforms carry texture, so a final art pass would want more level-object variety (erasers, washi tape, bottle caps as platforms). The jump pose's forward arms read a bit stiff. Character animation would also be the hard part in production: a sticker look tempts you toward cutout-puppet tweening, which can feel cheap unless frames are drawn with squash and stretch. At real scale the white border costs about 5px per character, so in a crowded 4-player pane the borders could merge into white clutter, and the border width would need tuning per zoom. The paint-as-sticker idea makes coverage very readable but less fluid and splashy than Splatoon's ink. The dark laptop lid limits backdrop variety, so other levels would need other surfaces (a lunchbox tin, a school folder) that are still low-contrast.
comps: Paper Mario: The Origami King / Sticker Star
Castle Crashers / Alien Hominid (Behemoth outlined chibis)
Cuphead-free mobile casual art (Kingdom Rush-style thick-outline chibi)
styles.anim: Natural fit is cutout/skeletal rigging (Spine, DragonBones or engine-side bone transforms): box head, rigid limbs and a single shared silhouette border mean parts can be rotated without redrawing, which is cheap. The risk is that tweened cutouts look like Flash-era web games; it needs squash-and-stretch on the head and a few hand-swapped key poses (run contact, jump tuck) to feel toy-like. A sticker-specific trick that is cheap and ownable: 'peel' flourishes (corner curl on spawn/death, a slap-down squash when landing or when paint lands). The die-cut border must be generated at runtime around the composited rig, otherwise each limb gets its own border and the single-sticker illusion breaks during rotation.
styles.engine: Good for the character side: flat-shaded vector parts export cleanly to grayscale-mask sprites (cap, overalls, reservoir, roller nap are clearly separated tint regions, and the pink/green variants prove it). The white die-cut border and drop shadow, however, cannot be baked per-part and look right; it needs either a post pass per character (render rig to offscreen target, dilate alpha, threshold, composite border + offset shadow) or pre-baked per-frame sprites with border included (which then fights runtime tinting only mildly, since the border is white). The paint is the harder fit: the concept's paint is a raised glossy band with bulbous drips on top of the surface edge; a runtime paint mask can do the fill, but the bead, drips and white sticker border around painted regions need an edge-detection/SDF shader over the paint mask plus a drip-spawn pass. Gloss can be a cheap highlight overlay. Shaders needed: alpha-dilate outline (or SDF), soft shadow, paint-mask edge bead/drips, optional brushed-metal backdrop texture (static image is fine).
strengths: Medium reads instantly: thick white borders + drop shadows on every gameplay object separate the play layer from the backdrop with zero ambiguity
Quarter-pane test genuinely passes: both painters, the spray, and blue vs orange coverage are legible at 480x270
Preserves the author's MS-Paint DNA (box head, dot eyes, flat line mouth, cap) so it is an upgrade of their identity rather than a replacement
Clean tint regions; pink and green variants already work, which is the real test of the random team-pair system
Dark low-detail backdrop is a strong neutral stage for any colour pair, and the faded backdrop stickers recede correctly
Flat vector shapes with a uniform outline treatment are within reach of a non-artist using vector tools or AI-assisted concepting then hand cleanup
Clear forward path for UI (sticker HUD, peel-off score reveals) that matches the user's 'gameplay first, UI follows' plan
risks: Paint does not read as paint: blue/orange bands look like tape or plastic strips laid on platforms, not ink that was sprayed; the gloss-sticker splat loses the messy, satisfying coverage feeling that is the core fantasy of a paint shooter

Paint contrast on the kraft/tan surface is fine for blue/orange but white sticker borders around paint plus white platform borders plus white character borders will compete; yellow (blue/yellow pair) on tan kraft is a likely weak case not shown
Painted coverage in the concept is hand-authored paths; a runtime mask will produce blocky or noisy edges unless the bead/drip edge shader is built, and that shader is the expensive, unproven part
White borders merge into clutter when 4 players overlap or stand on white-bordered platforms; border width must be tuned per zoom
Characters' faces are a bit blank and the jump pose is stiff; chunky designer-toy appeal depends on more expressive heads than shown
Scene is sparse and mostly flat beige rectangles; level variety (stationery props) is promised, not demonstrated
The 'sticker' conceit is a known casual-mobile look; without the peel/slap animation and physical-object staging it risks reading as generic vector clip-art
styles.verdict: A competent, readable concept that clearly beats the original on polish while keeping its box-head identity, and it passes the split-screen test comfortably; it is cheaper and more forgiving for a solo dev than detailed 16-bit pixel art. Its weak point is the thing that matters most in this game: paint looks like tidy stuck-on tape rather than splattered ink, and making painted coverage look this good at runtime needs a nontrivial edge/drip shader. The style's potential is higher than this execution (peel/slap animation, stationery-themed levels, sticker HUD), but as shown it reads as clean vector casual art more than a distinctive owned look.

identity.reason: It reads as casual-mobile vector work, and the paint reads as tape rather than splatter. The box-head lineage survives in name only.

production.reason: Readable, but every character needs a runtime dilate/border pass and paint needs a bead/drip SDF shader. The paint reads as tape, and the look slides toward generic mobile vector art.

player.reason: Characters are the most legible here thanks to the white die-cut border. The paint looks like tape strips, not splatter, which loses the paint-shooter fantasy, and the white borders will clutter with four players.

styles.name: Wet Gouache
styles.brief: Everything is painted in thick gouache/acrylic with visible brushstrokes and impasto — on-theme for a game about paint. Muted earthy world palette painted loosely; team paint is the freshest, wettest, most saturated paint in the frame, with glossy highlights. Characters are painted figures with chunky shapes.
styles.one_liner: A painter's studio painted loosely in matte, earthy gouache, where the box-headed painters and their paint are the only wet, glossy, fully saturated things on the canvas.
styles.ownable: It keeps the original MS-Paint figure's identity and doesn't swap it for a generic mascot. The box head, two dot eyes, flat line mouth, flat cap with brim and rectangular body are all still there. They're just rebuilt as chunky painted shapes with loose dark underpainting outlines, so anyone who knew the old stick figures will still recognise them. The medium is the game's theme: in a game about paint, the art is paint. The world is matte and dry-brushed and the team colours are glossy and wet, so the score (the coat of paint on the walkable tops) is the shiniest material in the frame. It reads at a glance, even in a quarter pane. Players have no ready comparison for it the way they do for 16-bit pixel art. The main reference points are storybook gouache backgrounds, and there's no crowded genre of games to stack it up against.
styles.self:
**What works:**
- The material contrast is the strongest part. The matte, dry-brushed umber platforms and the muted ochre/sage studio wall sit back, and the glossy blue and orange coats, droplets and splats jump forward. This holds clearly in the 480x270 squint test, where both players, the spray arc and every painted strip read straight away.
- The characters came out charming. At the 1.7x sheet scale they look like proper painted figures with personality, and they're a clear line from the original MS-Paint painter.
- The sheet's surface swatches (bare, team A, team B, contested edge) explain the scoring at a glance. The sprayer reads well large. The roller reads as a nappy cylinder with an end cap.

**Weak spots:**
- At the real in-game scale of about 118 px, the characters look more like a clean cartoon with an outline than like gouache. The brushwork mostly shows at sheet size, so a 4-player quarter pane would lose most of the medium on the figures.
- The backdrop's loose strokes partly read as random pale smudges, not deliberate painterly shapes. The window mullions and ladder still pick up a slight digital wobble from the displacement filters.
- Side-view paint coats are thin strips by nature, so 40 to 50% coverage looks lighter than it is.
- The impasto relief and dry-brush effects come from procedural filters. A real painted asset would have more intentional stroke direction and colour temperature shifts.
- Overall the world palette leans a bit muddy and brown. It sits right next to "dull", and an art pass would want more planned colour harmony, for example cooler shadows and warmer lit planes.

**File details:**
- scene.svg is about 352 KB, right at the ~350 KB cap.
- character.svg is about 283 KB.
- The final PNGs were rendered from the final SVGs.

All deliverables are in `the session scratchpad, concepts/gouache/`: scene.svg, scene.png, scene_small.png, character.svg and character.png.
comps: Splatoon (the mechanic and the wet-paint gloss, an instant comparison whatever the art style)
Cuphead (hand-painted backgrounds with outlined cartoon characters)
Okami (painting as the art and as the mechanic)
Castle Crashers / Alien Hominid (chunky outlined cartoon figures, which is what the characters read as at game scale)
Child of Light / Gris (painterly 2D, though watercolour rather than gouache)
styles.anim: The cheap, honest route is cut-out puppet rigs: flat painted parts (box head, cap, body, limbs, tool) with a separate greyscale mask for the team regions, animated on 2s, plus a few hand-painted key drawings for jump and land. A small looping displacement or texture jitter (boil) over the characters would carry the painted feel without repainting frames. Full frame-by-frame gouache for 4 players, 2+ weapons and every state is beyond a solo budget. Smooth skeletal tweening will expose that the figures are really flat vector shapes, so pose holds and stepped timing are required. The impasto and canvas look should be a screen-space post filter, not baked into each frame.
strengths: The material split is the real idea and it works: a matte, dry-brushed umber/ochre world against glossy, saturated team paint makes the score the shiniest thing on screen, and it survives the 480x270 squint test
Keeps the author's MS-Paint identity (box head, dot eyes, flat cap, rectangular body), so it reads as an evolution rather than a replacement
The medium is the theme: paint art in a paint game is a pitchable, ownable hook with no crowded genre to be ranked against, unlike 16-bit pixel art
Low-value, desaturated backdrop recedes well behind the action, which suits split-screen
Team colour is cleanly isolated to tintable regions, so it suits the existing runtime mask tinting
Painterly roughness forgives a non-artist's imprecision better than pixel art does
risks: At the real in-game size (~118 px, smaller in a 4-way quarter pane) the characters read as clean outlined cartoon, not gouache. The medium lives almost entirely in the world texture and post-filter, so the 'painted figures' claim is mostly unproven
The palette is muddy brown/beige and sits right next to 'dull'. The scene lacks a value or temperature plan and could read as drab in screenshots and store capsules

Untested pairs: yellow team paint on the ochre/beige wall and green paint over the sage dado band will lose much of the contrast blue/orange enjoys. The world palette will likely need to shift per pair or go cooler/greyer
The backdrop strokes read as random pale smudges, and the procedural wobble on straight elements (window mullions, ladder) looks digital rather than hand-made
Side-view coats are thin strips, so coverage looks lower than it is. Thicker coats or a stronger paint-side treatment may be needed for the score to read

Producing real painted assets at quality takes a painterly eye the author doesn't have. Using AI tools for concepts is fine, but keeping production art consistent across many level kits is the hard part
Needs new engine post-process and paint-material work. Without the shaders it degrades to generic flat vector
The wet-gloss paint invites a direct Splatoon comparison regardless of style
styles.verdict: The style has more potential than this execution shows. Matte world against glossy team paint is a strong, ownable, on-theme hook that keeps the box-head identity and reads in a quarter pane. The concept itself is middling: the gouache quality is mostly a procedural canvas filter over flat vector shapes, the characters look like ordinary outlined cartoons at game scale, and the world palette is muddy. It's worth pursuing over generic pixel art, but only with a deliberate colour plan (cooler shadows, testing all three team pairs, especially yellow) and a committed shader pass for grain, impasto and paint gloss.

identity.reason: It is on theme, but the world is muddy and brown, and the figures read as outlined cartoons at game scale. It also has the highest art-skill bar and needs new post-process work in Labrador.

production.reason: Painterly assets at consistent quality need a painter's eye. It also needs new post-process renderer work, and without it the look degrades to flat vector. The palette is muddy.

player.reason: Matte against gloss is a good idea, but the brown, muddy palette threatens yellow, green and orange teams. Paint coats are thin strips and the screenshot reads as drab.

styles.name: Crayon & Felt-tip
styles.brief: A child's drawing done well: waxy crayon fills with paper tooth showing through, felt-tip outlines, scribbled shading, wonky perspective. Characters are kid-drawn painters (round heads, stick limbs, hats). Team paint as poster paint blobs over the crayon.
styles.one_liner: A fridge-door drawing come to life: little round-headed painters in wax-crayon smocks and flat caps, drawn with wobbly felt-tip lines, slap thick, glossy poster paint across grey crayon blocks on cream paper, under a corner sun with a smiley face.
styles.ownable: It keeps the original game's look and polishes it instead of replacing it. The painter is still the author's MS-Paint character, with two dot eyes, a flat line mouth, a flat cap with a brim and stick limbs. It is redrawn as the best drawing a child could make, with a round crayon head, a team-coloured smock and felt-tip outlines that overshoot the corners. The grey platforms also come from the original. It suits the fiction because the painters are drawn in the same medium as the paint they use. Players can't file it under "another pixel-art game". The paint is the only fully saturated, glossy, opaque material in the picture, and everything else is waxy and full of paper texture. So the score (painted surface) is also the most eye-catching thing on screen. The team colour sits only in the cap and smock, and the bare surface is also neutral, so tinting by team at runtime is easy to keep separate.
styles.self:
**What came out well:**
- It reads at a glance as a child's drawing done well. It is easy to tell apart from pixel art and doodle styles.
- At 480x270 (one quarter of a 4-player split) both players and all the paint still stand out clearly against the muted world. The spray arc and the roller trail are readable.
- Painted versus bare surface is obvious, so the score is easy to read.
- The character sheet has real charm: the run and jump poses have energy, and the pink, green and blue variants show the team zones tint cleanly.
- It stays faithful to the original box-head painter.

**Weaknesses:**
- The procedural crayon texture is convincing at small sizes. Up close it still reads as noise rather than real wax drag, because there is no build-up where strokes overlap and no smearing.
- Because the platforms are deliberately neutral grey, the world is a bit plain and the middle of the scene is a lot of empty cream paper. That is good for gameplay contrast but makes for a quiet backdrop. A real art pass would want themed props or a few more child-style background stories, while keeping them at low pressure.
- The sprayer in the player's hands is tiny at game scale, so the paint bottle's fill level isn't readable in play.
- The roller drum at 1:1 reads as an orange blob rather than a cylinder.
- The ramp is simplistic.
- This concept can't show motion. The style probably needs line boil (redrawn wobble frames) in motion to feel truly hand-made. Without it, crisp vector sprites sliding around could look like a filter rather than a drawing.
styles.anim: The right method is frame-by-frame line boil: 2-3 redrawn wobble frames per pose, cycled at about 8-12 fps. Stick limbs and a round head make the poses cheap to draw. Each pose takes about 4-8 frames, plus the boil copies. The character is so simple that a cutout rig (head, smock, two-segment limbs) would also work, as long as a boil texture or wobble shader runs on top. Without boil the vector-crisp sprites will slide around like stickers and the "drawn by hand" read falls apart. That is the main motion risk. Paint drips can be a few looping decal frames. The cost stays low because there are no shading ramps and no facial animation beyond dot eyes and a line mouth.
styles.engine: The fit is good. The team colour sits only in the cap, the smock and the paint. The sheet already splits these out as a flat tintable zone over a fixed greyscale crayon texture, which maps directly onto the grayscale team-mask tint. To keep the wax texture under the tint, the mask should be authored as greyscale crayon strokes rather than flat grey. Runtime paint fits as a tinted coverage mask over surface top edges, with drip decals and a gloss/sheen pass. That needs a small shader or a pre-made sheen overlay. The paper grain should be a screen- or world-space overlay shader, or a multiplied texture, so it does not swim with sprites. A cheap per-frame UV jitter of a noise texture could fake line boil on static geometry. No halftone is needed. Without shaders it still works as plain sprites, just flatter.
strengths: It grows directly out of the author's own MS-Paint box-head painter. The identity is earned, not borrowed, and the character sheet has real charm. Idle, run and jump all read with personality.

The materials are split well. The glossy, saturated, opaque poster paint is the only material of its kind on screen, against waxy, desaturated crayon, so painted vs bare surface (the score) is the most obvious thing in the frame.
The quarter-pane test (480x270) holds up. The paint bands, the spray arc and both team colours read instantly.
The team zone is limited to the cap and smock, which makes runtime tinting simple and robust across the pink/green and blue variants shown.
It is forgiving. Wobble and imprecision read as intent, so a non-artist's roughness becomes a feature instead of a flaw.
It sits far from the crowded 16-bit pixel-art field.
risks: The scene undersells the sheet. In-game the characters are small and spindly, and the crayon fill on the smocks mostly vanishes, so they look like generic thin doodle figures. The charm lives at sheet scale. The characters need to be bigger relative to the world, or have chunkier limbs and heads.

The world reads more as a neat felt-tip/vector diagram than a child's crayon drawing. The platforms are tidy grey brick boxes with clean perspective, and a large empty cream field fills the middle. The 'child's drawing done well' energy shows only in the sun and clouds.
The procedural crayon texture looks like noise, not wax. The ground hatching turns into busy static at quarter size, which competes with the paint near the floor.
The yellow team colour on cream paper (the blue/yellow pair) is untested and will likely lose contrast against the paper and the sun. Orange also comes close to the sun's warm tones.
There is no motion proof. Without line boil, crisp sprites sliding over textured paper can look like a Photoshop filter.
The sprayer and the roller drum are illegible at game scale. Weapon identity relies on silhouette that isn't there yet.
Producing real crayon assets (scanned or Krita brushes) consistently across a full game is a discipline problem for a solo dev. Mixing procedural and hand-made textures will show.
styles.verdict: The style itself is strong and the right kind of ownable. It grows from the author's own crude painter, it is forgiving to execute, and it naturally makes glossy poster paint the hero material, so the score reads well even in a quarter pane. This execution is only middling. The character sheet is charming, but the in-game scene shrinks the painters to thin doodles and draws the world as tidy grey brick boxes on empty paper, which reads closer to a clean vector diagram than a crayon drawing. On potential it scores about an 8; this concept is about a 6. It deserves another pass with bigger, chunkier characters, a messier hand-drawn world, a yellow-team test and a boil-animation check before anyone judges it against the pixel-art candidate.

identity.reason: The character sheet has charm, but in game the painters shrink to thin doodles on tidy grey boxes. The head also changes to a round one, which is a step away from the box-head identity.

production.reason: Forgiving, but it needs line boil, which multiplies frame counts, and keeping crayon texture consistent across a whole game is a discipline problem. The scene undersells it.

player.reason: The sheet has charm, but in-game the figures are spindly. The ground hatching becomes static next to the paint, and yellow sits on cream.

styles.name: Doodled Painters on a Painted World
styles.brief: MIX. Characters and weapons: the ORIGINAL box-head hat stick figures, redrawn as crisp black ink line doodles (white fill, confident line). Environment: a loose wet gouache painted world (muted, brushy, earthy). The flat white doodle characters read crisply against the painterly background, like an animator's pencil test over a painted backdrop. Team paint is saturated wet paint.
styles.one_liner: The 2022 box-head painters come back as confident black-ink doodles with white fill, running across a muted, brushy gouache landscape and leaving glossy wet team paint dripping off every ledge they cover.
styles.ownable: It keeps the author's original character, redrawn rather than replaced. The box head, two dot eyes, flat mouth, brimmed cap, rectangular body and single-line limbs are all still there, and so is the roller drawn end-on as a stick and a circle. The figures are now drawn in clean ink with overshooting corners, and the world behind them is opaque matte gouache in earthy ochre, sage and umber. Putting a deliberately "unfinished" pencil-test character over a finished painted backdrop is uncommon in games. Players have no obvious pixel-art comparison for it; the closest reference point is an animator's desk, not another game. Team paint is the only fully saturated colour on screen, glossy and dripping, so the score surface always stands out. The tint regions are cleanly separable: the cap, splats and hem on the body, the sprayer's reservoir (whose fill level can show ammo), and the roller's drum. Everything else on the character is white or black, so any of the random team colour pairs will drop in.
styles.self:
What works:
- The mix reads at a glance. The white ink figures pop clearly off the painterly world.
- At 480x270 (quarter pane) both players, the spray arc and every painted surface stay legible. Blue and orange are the loudest things in the frame.
- The character is unmistakably the original box-head painter, and the sheet makes the tint regions explicit.
- The gouache sky and clouds are convincing, and the rolled trail and the dripping spray paint read as two different paint types.

Weaknesses:
- The midground haze under the hills drifts toward soft digital fog rather than crisp opaque gouache. Real gouache would have harder-edged colour shapes.
- Platform slabs carry their brush texture but are fairly plain blocks.
- The wet-paint specular highlight sometimes gives the blue a slightly glassy look.
- On the sprayer pose, the reservoir sits against the chest and can read as a blue pouch.
- The surface swatches are modest.
- The concept cannot show the medium's main risk, which is motion. Static ink figures look intentional, but in-game they need hand-drawn frames (or line boil) or they will look like flat clip-art over a painting.
- The muted world also has to stay muted on every stage, or the white figures lose their pop.
comps: Splatoon (the paint mechanic is the unavoidable comparison, but the art is nothing like it)
a-ha 'Take On Me' video / Who Framed Roger Rabbit (pencil-line figure over a rendered world; the closest reference for the look)
Crayon Physics Deluxe / Drawn to Life (drawn-on-a-page feel)
Cuphead (only on the question of hand-drawn line animation quality)
styles.anim: The characters are box-and-line figures, so frame-by-frame animation is cheap. A run cycle is about 6-8 frames of a box and four lines. Drawing on 2s with slight line boil (2-3 redraws of each pose) makes stiffness look intentional, and for this style that is close to required: if a static doodle is moved by a cutout rig it looks like clip-art slid over a painting, which the artist already flags. A cutout rig with procedural line jitter in a shader is a cheaper fallback, but it looks weaker. Weapons work as separate overlay sprites. The roller works as a rotating circle sprite with a stick. The tint mask is cap + hem/splats + reservoir/drum, authored as its own layer. Backgrounds are static parallax layers, and at most a slow cloud drift is needed. Most of the motion budget goes on the paint: drips that extend over time, splat particles, and the different look of rolled versus sprayed paint.
styles.engine: Characters fit the tint-at-draw engine very well. They are mostly pure white fill and black ink, so the team-colour mask is a small separate grayscale layer (cap, hem, splats, reservoir, drum), and any team pair drops in cleanly, as the sheet shows. Ink width is meant to stay constant in screen pixels, which will break under camera zoom or different pane sizes. That needs line-weight variants per scale, or keeping sprite scale fixed per pane. Backgrounds are opaque painted layers plus tileable slab face and edge strips, which a sprite engine handles fine. Painted surfaces are the shader work. Runtime paint should be a coverage mask render target, drawn with (a) an edge-displacement/noise pass for organic edges, (b) drips grown down from coverage edges on ledges, and (c) a cheap fake-specular gloss band, since real lighting is not needed. A full-screen paper-grain overlay on the environment only (not on characters or paint) is a cheap optional pass, and it is what sells 'gouache'. No halftone is needed. The roller-versus-spray difference needs two brush stamp types in the paint writer.
strengths: It keeps the author's own character (box head, dot eyes, flat mouth, brimmed cap, end-on roller) and gives it a confident, deliberate line. This is the only kind of direction that keeps the 'weird but real identity' instead of replacing it.

The value structure is right for a paint game. The world is muted mid-value and earthy, characters are near-pure white with black outlines, and team paint is the only saturated colour on screen. In the 480x270 test both players and every painted ledge are still clearly readable.
Painted surfaces read as material: dripping, glossy, sitting on top of dark umber slabs. Rolled paint (an even band) and sprayed paint (drips plus splatter) are different enough to read as two types.
Clean tint separation (everything not white or black is a team region) suits the grayscale-mask engine and random team pairs.
Low comparison exposure. Nobody will set it beside a famous game and call it a worse version, unlike 16-bit pixel art.
Characters are cheap for a non-artist to author and animate, and roughness reads as intentional.
risks: The world comes out as a sepia, foggy haze. The midground (hills, trees, house) is washed into soft digital fog, and the whole frame looks like it has a brown filter on it. The result is muddy and dreary rather than painterly. The brief only asked for 'muted', and right now it is drab. Real gouache needs harder, flat opaque colour shapes and more value range.

Contrast depends on the team pair. Yellow paint against the ochre/khaki sky and sand tones, and green paint against the sage midground, will lose a lot of pop. Only blue and orange are shown in the scene. Paint on the dark umber slabs is safe for every pair, but airborne spray and splats against the sky are not.

Characters are small, about 6-7% of frame height. At quarter pane the figures are tiny white specks with a coloured cap, and facing and weapon are barely readable. That is acceptable for locating players but weak for reading what they are doing.
Motion is unproven. Without hand-drawn frames or line boil it collapses into clip-art over a painting.

The backgrounds are the expensive, skill-dependent part. A solo non-artist making good gouache backdrops per stage is the real bar, and AI-generated painted backdrops are the obvious temptation, with a consistency and maintainability cost.
Platform slabs are plain dark blocks. Gameplay geometry is legible but has no character, so stages could feel samey.
The wet-paint specular can look glassy or plastic, which conflicts with the matte gouache world.
Constant screen-space line width conflicts with any camera zoom.
styles.verdict: This is the strongest kind of answer to the author's dilemma. It keeps the original box-head painters, tidies them into confident ink doodles, and puts them in a world quiet enough that team paint is clearly the loudest thing on screen. That value hierarchy is correct for a game scored on painted area. The execution is mid-grade. The gouache world is a brown, foggy sepia wash rather than crisp opaque paint, the slabs are plain, and yellow or green team pairs will fight the ochre and sage palette. The style itself has clear potential: it is cheap on characters, hard to compare against anything famous, and its main real costs are good painted backdrops and a hand-drawn animation pass.

identity.reason: The ink-doodle painters keep the original figure. Per the critique, the gouache world comes out as a brown sepia fog, and painted backdrops are the skill the author lacks. That puts the cost in the wrong place for a solo non-artist.

production.reason: The characters are cheap, but good gouache backdrops for every stage are the expensive, skill-bound part, and this one already reads as muddy sepia fog.

player.reason: The white figures pop, but the sepia fog world is drab. Yellow and green will fight the ochre and sage palette, and it would make a muddy capsule.

styles.name: Paint.exe Figures on a Riso World
styles.brief: MIX. Characters and weapons: the ORIGINAL crude MS-Paint box-head hat stick figures (aliased, white fill, black lines). Environment: a risograph-printed world (dark navy/charcoal key ink, halftones, misregistration, paper grain) matching the existing menu art. Team paint printed as fluoro spot ink.
styles.one_liner: The author's own aliased Paint.exe box-head painters, unchanged and untextured, pasted onto a dark navy risograph print of a giant paint workshop where every coat of team paint is a misregistered fluoro spot ink.
styles.ownable: It keeps the game's one real piece of identity, the original crude MS-Paint figure (box head, dot eyes, flat mouth, brimmed cap, rectangle body, the bent arm line drawn inside the body), and the original roller, which is still just a line and a circle. It then makes that crudeness look deliberate by setting it against a world that is clearly crafted: navy key ink like the existing menu art, varying-size halftone faces, off-register slate under-prints, paper grain. Players have no ready comparison: it isn't pixel art, vector-flat or hand-painted. It reads as a zine with MS-Paint stickers on it. The concept says outright that the figures are Paint.exe but the paint they throw is real ink: once paint leaves the nozzle it becomes riso. That makes the score surface the most print-like and most vivid thing on screen. Small charms carry the low-fi voice: the hat lags off the head when jumping, and the overalls carry a Paint.exe airbrush speckle of team colour.
styles.self:
What works: the two halves are distinct at a glance. The pure-white aliased figures pop hard against the navy at 1600 and still read as white bodies with team-coloured caps in the 480x270 quarter-pane test. The paint is the brightest, most saturated thing on screen and sits on the cream walkable tops, so painted versus unpainted is obvious. Coverage is about 48%. The background stays quiet. The sheet shows idle/run/jump in blue and orange plus pink, green and yellow variants, large weapons, and three coverage swatches.

Weaknesses: at true in-game scale (120 px) the figures and especially the roller head are small. At quarter-pane size the roller becomes an orange dot, and P1's sprayer arc is a thin line. Weapons may need to be oversized compared with the original art. The cream platform faces with heavy halftone are fairly bright and busy, so with many platforms they could start to compete. A darker paper ink for faces is worth testing. Blue paint in mid-air over navy relies on the paper-gap ghost and is the weakest team colour against this world; yellow and green would be very loud. The deep-ground solid fill is a slightly different tone from the halftone ramp above it, so a faint seam shows. Only one riso key colour is explored (no second spot ink in the environment such as the menu art's mint). The static concept can't show whether halftone faces shimmer when the camera scrolls. Files: the session scratchpad, concepts/mix_mspaint_riso/scene.svg (310 KB), character.svg (224 KB), scene.png, scene_small.png, character.png, and gen.py.
comps: Splatoon (the mechanic, so every paint read will be compared to it)
Kingdom of Loathing / West of Loathing (crude stick figures as deliberate identity)
styles.anim: The figures are on a 52x120 aliased grid with a few hard-edged limbs, so animation is cheap frame-by-frame redrawing in Paint or Aseprite, about 4-6 frames for each of run, jump and idle. Choppiness reads as intentional, and staying at low frame counts (8-12 fps) fits. The hat lagging off the head on a jump is a cheap secondary-motion charm: it can be a separate sprite on a one-frame delay. Weapons can be separate attached sprites, so there is no rigging. The world is static parallax plates, which cost nothing to animate. Paint drips could be a simple shader or a few-frame overlay. Avoid any line boil on the figures, since jitter would make Paint.exe aliasing look broken rather than deliberate.
styles.engine: The engine fit is very good for the figures. They are literally white fill plus black line, with the hat, tank, roller sleeve and speckle as single tint regions, so they map directly onto grayscale-mask tinting at draw time. Each figure is one sprite plus one mask. The world can be pre-printed parallax plates plus tiling platform textures with the halftone baked in. Paint needs a little shader work: (1) sample a dot-screen or edge-noise when compositing the runtime coverage texture, (2) draw a paper-coloured offset ghost (2-3 px) for misregistration, and (3) optionally multiply the platform halftone over the paint so it reads as overprinted. The full-screen paper grain should be a screen-space overlay anchored to the screen, not the world, so it does not swim. It should be reduced or disabled per pane at quarter size, because at 480x270 it turns into visible noise. The halftone on platform faces must be baked at integer scale or kept world-locked to avoid moire and shimmer when the camera scrolls. That is the main technical risk.
strengths: Keeps the author's one real piece of identity, the box-head capped figure, intact, and the crafted print world makes its crudeness read as a deliberate choice rather than an amateur one
White figures with black outlines pop very hard against the navy key ink; this is the strongest player silhouette contrast of any approach on this background
Painted versus unpainted is clear at full size: paint sits on cream walkable tops, and the dark-ink background never competes with it
No ready comparison as a whole: it is not pixel art, flat vector or hand-painted, so the comparison bar is low
Very cheap for a solo non-artist: figures are drawable in literally MS Paint, and the world is a few plates plus shaders
The team tint is perfectly isolated in the hat, tank, sleeve and speckle, which fits the engine's grayscale mask tinting exactly
The character sheet is the best piece: at 2.6x the aliased figures look charming and confident, and the hat lag and airbrush speckle carry the voice
risks: At quarter-pane size the figures are about 12px wide. The roller becomes an orange dot, and the sprayer stream is only legible because of its arc. Weapons, and maybe the figures, likely need about 1.5x oversizing over the originals

Blue paint over navy is the weak pair. In mid-air the blue stream nearly disappears into the background at small size, and the paper-ghost trick is too subtle to save it. Blue/orange and blue/yellow both hit this
Paper grain at 480x270 reads as TV static or noise over the whole pane. It must scale down or disappear in split-screen
The cream halftone platform faces are the second-brightest thing on screen. In a dense level they will compete with the paint and make the scene look busy

The scene itself is a little sparse and floaty: platforms on thin trestles in a large empty navy field, and the deep-ground slab joins the halftone ramp with a visible tonal seam. As a level mock-up it is less convincing than the character sheet
Halftone shimmer or moire under camera scroll is untested and is the main production unknown
Only one environment ink is used. Over a full game the navy-only world may feel monotonous unless the stages rotate second inks, like the menu art's mint
The style split (crude figures over crafted print) only works if the world is clearly crafted. If the riso world is executed weakly, the whole thing collapses into looking amateur
styles.verdict: This is the most ownable direction for the author because it keeps the real identity, the Paint.exe box-head, and gives it a deliberate frame that is cheap to produce and fits the tint-mask engine almost perfectly. The style has more potential than this execution shows. The character sheet is strong, but the scene is sparse and weak at quarter-pane size: the grain turns to noise, the roller vanishes, and blue paint gets lost on navy. Weapon oversizing, a split-screen grain cutoff and a lighter or different world key ink for blue matches are needed before this proves itself.

identity.reason: This is the only concept that keeps the author's actual figure: aliased white fill, black line, box head, flat cap, and a roller that is 'a line and a circle, as it always was'. It frames that figure in a crafted print world, so the crudeness reads as a choice. The character sheet (hat lag, airbrush speckle) has the most soul of the whole batch. White figures on dark key ink have the strongest player silhouette of any concept, and the world ties directly to the existing halftone/navy/orange menu art. That matters because the user wants the UI to follow the gameplay look. I checked the small render. Blue paint on navy is weak, and the grain turns to static at 480x270. Both are fixable by changing the key ink and tuning the grain, not by changing direction.

production.reason: White figures pop hard against navy, and the figures themselves cost almost nothing. But the full-pane grain turns to TV static at 480x270, blue paint gets lost on navy, and the world half carries the craft burden. If it looks weak, the mix collapses into looking amateur.

player.reason: The white figures pop on navy, and paint on the cream tops reads. Blue paint in the air disappears into the navy, so blue, the most common team, suffers. The grain looks like TV static at pane size, and the weapons vanish.

styles.name: Pixel Painters in a Paper Diorama
styles.brief: MIX. Characters and weapons: crisp low-res pixel-art painters (overalls, cap, gloves — like the current workshop pixel candidate; draw them as visible square pixels using <rect>s, ~13x30 pixel grid scaled up). Environment: a layered cut-paper/cardboard diorama with torn edges and depth shadows. Pixel figures as if they were tiny printed stickers living in a craft-paper world.
styles.one_liner: Tiny die-cut pixel-painter stickers running across a hand-built cardboard diorama, where paint flies as hard pixel squares and lands as torn, white-cored scraps of coloured paper glued onto corrugated platforms.
styles.ownable: The two-medium rule carries the gameplay itself. Anything that belongs to a player (the painter, the weapon, paint in flight) is crisp pixel art printed as a stepped die-cut sticker with a white border and a lifted shadow. Anything that belongs to the world (platforms, backdrop, and paint once it has landed) is torn paper and cut cardboard. So the score surface reads as a physical craft material: a pixel droplet hardens into a torn tissue splat on contact. The environment details are specific rather than generic: chipboard slabs with the corrugated flute showing on the cut face, cream top sheets with torn white lips, masking tape, wooden skewer supports, cut-paper clouds and paint tins hung on threads, and faded red "this way up" box stamps on the floor. Players have no ready comparison for it. It isn't "another 16-bit game" or "another papercraft game". It's pixel stickers in a shoebox, and the low-res sprites keep a direct line back to the original MS-Paint box-head painter (cap brim, dot eyes, flat mouth).
styles.self:
What works:
- Both images read clearly. The split between pixel actors and paper world is immediate.
- At 480x270 the two players stay distinct (the white sticker rim does most of that work), and blue and orange paint on the cream platform tops reads clearly as score.
- The muted blue-grey and kraft backdrop sits back without competing.
- Corrugated cut faces, tape, skewers and threaded clouds sell "handmade diorama" well.
- The white-cored torn paint strips look like paper, not liquid.
- About half the walkable tops are painted, split between teams, with a visible front line on the middle platform.

Weaknesses:
- The paint scraps are thin (about 16 px). In a quarter pane they read as coloured lines, not regions, so a production pass should make the paint layer thicker or let it wrap the platform lip.
- The pixel painters themselves are fairly conventional pixel art. The style's identity comes from the sticker treatment and the mix, so the "generic pixel art" worry is reduced, not removed.
- The flat line mouth under the dot eyes reads a bit like a moustache.
- The jump pose arms look a little antler-like.
- The roller is legible but chunky. Its orange head merges with the orange trail it leaves.
- The backdrop is quite quiet. The upper third is mostly empty paper and threads, which is good for readability but low on spectacle.

Files are in the session scratchpad, concepts/mix_pixel_collage/:
- scene.svg (150 KB)
- character.svg (292 KB)
- scene.png, scene_small.png and character.png, all rendered from the final SVGs
comps: Paper Mario: Sticker Star / Color Splash (sticker-in-papercraft, and Color Splash is literally painting a paper world)
Yoshi's Crafted World (cardboard diorama, 'this way up' box craft)
Kirby's Epic Yarn / Kirby and the Rainbow Curse (material-world platformers)
Super Mario Bros. sprites (cap + overalls + moustache-like mouth reads as Mario/Luigi)
Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game / generic 16-bit pixel brawlers for the sprites alone
styles.anim: The sprites are frame-by-frame pixel art on a small ~13x30 grid. That is cheap per frame and a solo dev can manage it in Aseprite: about 4-8 frames per state, with idle/run/jump/roll plus weapon overlays. The sticker border and lifted shadow should be a runtime dilate-and-offset pass so it isn't baked into every frame. That keeps the per-frame art cost at plain-pixel level. The papercraft world mostly doesn't animate. Optional extras are a slight sway on threaded clouds and tins, and a 'peel' or flutter on paint tabs. Landed paint is the costly part. It has to grow as torn paper at runtime, so it needs a procedural torn-edge mask, drip tabs spawned at platform lips, and maybe a white under-core offset. Paint in flight is just pixel squares, which costs almost nothing.
styles.engine: Good for actors. Team colour sits in four isolated ramps (cap, overalls, sprayer tank, roller nap), which maps straight onto grayscale-mask tinting at draw time. Pixel projectiles fit too: they are tinted squares. The sticker rim is best done as a sprite shader, a 1-texel dilation in off-white plus an offset soft shadow, or as a pre-baked outline layer that stays untinted. The world wants a paper-grain/mottle overlay that applies to background and platforms only, not to stickers, so it needs either a layer-ordered full-screen multiply or grain baked into the environment textures. The runtime painted surface is the real work. Torn-paper paint means the coverage mask has to be rendered with a tileable torn-edge alpha texture (noise-thresholded border) plus a white rim offset. Drips/tabs have to be emitted as decals at platform edges. Doable as one custom paint-surface shader, but more involved than a flat tinted fill.
strengths: The two-medium rule is a real idea, not decoration: player-owned things are crisp pixel stickers and world-owned things are paper. Landed paint switches to the paper medium, so 'paint became world = score' gets explained visually.
The white die-cut rim separates the players from a busy background extremely well. Even at 480x270 both painters pop instantly.
The quiet, desaturated kraft and blue-grey backdrop leaves the saturated team colours as the loudest things on screen.

The environment details are specific and charming: corrugated flute on the cut faces, skewer supports, masking tape, threaded clouds, faded box stamps. Together they read as one handmade shoebox, not generic papercraft.

Production split is sensible for a solo dev: small pixel sprites (cheap, tintable) plus a mostly static layered diorama that can come from scans, photographed real cardboard, or AI concepts cleaned into layers.
In-flight pixel squares turning into landed torn paper is a readable, ownable gameplay VFX hook.
risks: Paint coverage is the weakest element. It is a thin strip on platform tops, and in the quarter pane it reads as coloured lines, not owned territory. For a game scored on surface area this is the main readability failure. Paint has to be thicker, wrap the lip, or stain the cut face.

Colour-pair fragility: the platform tops are cream and the world is kraft/tan. Orange already sits close to the kraft hue, and the yellow team in the blue/yellow pair will nearly vanish on cream tops. The pink/green pair is fine. The world palette may need to be cooler or greyer, or the paint needs a dark under-edge.

The sprites read as Mario/Luigi knock-offs: cap, overalls, and a dot-eyes-plus-line mouth that reads as a moustache. That pulls in the most famous comparison in games and loses the MS-Paint box-head lineage the author values. The face needs redesigning, e.g. a boxier head or no mouth line.

The 'pixel sprite on painted/crafted background' look has precedent (indie mixed-media games and Paper Mario stickers). The identity rests heavily on the torn-paper paint treatment landing in-engine. If it ships as flat fills, it collapses to 'pixel art on a beige background'.
The players are tiny relative to the frame (about 1/12 of screen height). In a 4-pane split that is roughly 18-20 px tall, and the roller and jump poses (antler arms) lose legibility.
The orange roller head merges into its own orange trail, so weapon and paint blur together for that team.
Grain and vignette overlays plus the diorama depth shadows may cost clarity in split-screen. Keep them subtle and tunable.
styles.verdict: The concept is coherent and more ownable than straight 16-bit pixel art. Pixel stickers in a cardboard shoebox, with paint that hardens into torn paper on landing, is a genuine idea that ties the art to the scoring rule. It is also realistically buildable by a solo developer. The execution falls short where it matters most for this game. Landed paint is a thin line that won't read as territory at quarter-pane size. The cream and kraft world will struggle with orange and especially yellow teams. The cap, overalls and moustache-like mouth make the painters read as Mario. Worth pursuing if the paint layer is made much bolder, the world palette is cooled to protect warm team colours, and the painters' faces are redrawn closer to the original box-head design.

identity.reason: The pixel painters read as a Mario/Luigi knock-off: cap, overalls and a mouth like a moustache. That reopens the pixel comparison trap, and the thin paint strip does not read as territory.

production.reason: Pixel sprites keep the high bar of pixel art. Landed paint is a thin line that doesn't read as territory, the painters read as Mario, and torn-paper paint needs a custom shader.

player.reason: Coverage is a thin line, not territory. The kraft and cream world swallows orange and yellow, and the sprites read as Mario.

styles.name: Sticker Painters on Blueprints
styles.brief: MIX. Characters and weapons: glossy die-cut vinyl sticker characters with thick white borders (designer-toy proportions). Environment: graphite technical drawing on off-white drafting paper (construction lines, dimensions, hatching). Avoid blue backgrounds (team colour). Team paint lands as real paint on the drawing.
styles.one_liner: Glossy die-cut vinyl painters, box heads and flat caps, peeled and stuck onto a pencil engineering drawing of the arena, then sprayed with real wet paint where they have scored.
styles.ownable: There are three separate materials, and each one has a single job. The world is a graphite technical drawing: section-hatched platforms, dimension lines ("4500", "3820 CLR"), dash-dot centrelines and faint ghost elevations of a spray gun and a paint tin. The players are physical die-cut stickers with a thick white border, a cast shadow and a vinyl gloss highlight. The paint is real, wet and glossy, sitting on top of the drawing with drips running down the platform faces. That makes the gameplay rule visible: anything that is still graphite has not been scored yet. The painter keeps the original MS-Paint identity (box head, two dot eyes, flat line mouth, flat cap with a brim) and moves it into designer-toy proportions, so it reads as an evolution of the author's figure rather than a replacement. I can't think of an obvious game to compare it with. Small details carry the joke without competing with play: a "SURFACE: PAINTABLE" leader note and a dashed "trajectory" construction curve under the sprayer stream. The team colours are confined to the cap, overall bib and legs, the backpack reservoir's paint level, the gun's pressure chamber and the roller drum, so runtime tinting stays separable. The sheet shows this working for blue, orange, pink and green.
styles.self: What worked: the three-material split reads instantly. In the 480x270 quarter-pane render the players and the paint are by far the loudest elements, and the drafting world falls back while the platform tops stay readable as walkable lines. The stickers look tactile and appealing, the box-head lineage is clear, and the score paint reads unmistakably as being on the surfaces. Weaknesses: (1) The jump pose is weak. With tucked legs and a raised arm it reads more like a crouch than airborne, and it needs a proper stretched leap. (2) The run poses for idle and run are close, because the run lean is only 9 degrees, and they could be more extreme. (3) The roller in the scene is short-handled at gameplay scale compared with the sheet. (4) The arena is deliberately airy, but it may feel empty; a real level would want more drafting incident, like stair runs, section callouts and scale bars, kept at low contrast. (5) The white sticker border adds about 6 px around every player, which makes the collision silhouette look wider than 52 units; that would need to be settled with gameplay. (6) The dimension text and labels are environment art, not UI, but with a later UI pass they could be confused with HUD, so the UI should borrow the drafting language carefully.
comps: Splatoon (paint drips and the gloss on the score paint)
Paper Mario: Sticker Star / The Origami King (die-cut sticker characters with white borders)
Crayon Physics Deluxe and Line Rider (hand-drawn lines on paper as the world)
Bridge Constructor / Poly Bridge (blueprint and engineering-drawing framing)
Fancy Pants Adventures (sketchy paper world with a bold character on top)
Generic flat-vector mobile mascot games (Subway Surfers stickers, Brawl Stars promo sticker packs), which is where the characters drift
styles.anim: Rigid stickers are the natural fit for a cutout rig: separate head, cap, torso, limbs and weapon, rotated as whole pieces. A sticker is supposed to be stiff, so a limited rig reads as intentional and does not look cheap. A "peel and wobble" squash on landing or a hit would be a cheap, on-brand flourish. Frame-by-frame would be wasted on this look. There is a catch: the die-cut white border has to wrap the whole silhouette in every frame. If each rig part carries its own border, you get white seams at the joints. So either bake the border per pose at export, or generate it at runtime as a dilated-alpha outline pass over the composited character (a render-to-texture of the character, then a dilate and a shadow). The sheet's poses are timid: idle, run and jump are nearly the same silhouette, as the artist admits. A real rig would need much stronger key poses to sell motion at quarter-pane scale. The drafting world is static and could get a subtle line-boil, but that is optional.
styles.engine: Characters fit well. Team colour is confined to the cap, bib, legs, tank fill, chamber and drum, all flat fills, so grayscale team masks tinted at draw time work cleanly. The four-colour sheet shows the separation already holds. The sticker border plus drop shadow should be baked into the sprite, or done as an outline post-pass on a per-character RT, not live SVG morphology. The world is the harder part. Graphite lines, hatching and dimension annotations need either hand-authored tile or atlas art per platform size, or a procedural line/hatch renderer with a screen-space paper-grain overlay. That is a simple shader, plus a pencil-tooth multiply. Runtime paint fits the existing surface-painting model, but this concept's version is a wet, raised, specular paint band with spawned drip decals. Reproducing that needs a normal or height-derived gloss shader over the coverage mask, plus drip decals at ledge edges. A flat-tinted coverage mask will look noticeably cheaper than the concept. The off-white paper is a real problem for one shipped pair. Yellow paint on #ebe5d3 will have weak contrast, so the yellow teams need a darker outline or rim on the paint, or a deeper yellow/ochre.
strengths: The three-material split (graphite world, vinyl characters, wet paint) makes the scoring rule legible: anything still pencil is unclaimed. That is a real gameplay-art idea, not just decoration.
The paint is the best thing in the concept. Glossy, dripping and raised, it reads clearly as being on the surfaces, and it pops for blue, orange, pink and green.
The drafting world steps back politely and leaves the players and paint as the loudest elements. It avoids blue, as briefed.
The die-cut white border gives every character a free, very strong silhouette separation against any background. That holds up even at quarter-pane size.
Team-colour regions are cleanly separable for runtime mask tinting, and that is shown on four colourways.
Characters are flat vector shapes: authorable in Inkscape or Affinity by a non-artist and riggable as cutouts.
The drafting environment (dimension lines, section hatching, "SURFACE: PAINTABLE") is a fairly unclaimed look for a paint shooter and has room for jokes.
risks: The characters have been sanded smooth. The original MS-Paint box-head's charm came from crudeness. These are polished flat-vector mascots with blush cheeks and a cap highlight, which sit squarely in generic mobile-sticker territory. The lineage survives, the weirdness mostly does not.

In the 480x270 test the platforms nearly disappear. Thin, low-contrast graphite lines with faint hatching make the walkable geometry the weakest-reading element. The dimension text and labels turn into grey noise that looks like UI. Playable geometry needs heavier line weight or a darker top edge than the concept uses.
Yellow paint (the blue/yellow pair) on cream paper will have poor contrast, and the concept never tests it.
The wet-paint look depends on specular lighting and drip decals. A plain tinted coverage mask will lose most of the appeal, so the shader work is load-bearing.
The white sticker border makes the characters read about 10-15% wider than their collision box. It also looks odd when characters overlap each other or the paint (white halos over the paint).
The airy arena reads as empty. A real level needs more drafting incident, and every added line competes with platform readability.
Weak pose language in the jump, run and idle frames, and the roller is undersized in the scene.
styles.verdict: This is the strongest idea in the concept: a graphite blueprint world where only the scored surfaces get real wet paint, which makes the score visible at a glance. The paint execution is genuinely good. The weak points are characters that slide from the author's odd box-head into polished but generic vector-mascot sticker art, and platforms that nearly vanish at quarter-pane scale. Keep the world-and-paint material split, make the platform top edges much heavier, test yellow on the paper, and roughen the stickers back toward the MS-Paint figure. As executed it is a solid 7. The style has more potential than this sheet shows.

identity.reason: The paint and the world are good, but the stickers have been sanded down into mobile-mascot art with blush cheeks. That is the exact loss of crude identity the author fears, and the platforms disappear at quarter-pane size.
