production.reason: It has two shader dependencies (sticker border and gloss paint), platforms that vanish at quarter pane, and characters polished into generic mascots.

player.reason: The paint is good, but the platforms disappear at pane size, the dimension text reads as UI noise, and the characters are generic mascots.

styles.name: Bold Cartoon on Ink Wash
styles.brief: MIX. Characters and weapons: bold, thick-outlined flat-colour cartoon painters with expressive simple shapes (team colour on clothing). Environment: monochrome sumi ink-wash world on rice paper. Colour lives only on characters and paint — the world stays grey so both players and score read instantly.
styles.one_liner: Chunky, thick-outlined cartoon painters with box heads and flat caps sprint across floating sumi-ink crags on rice paper. The only colour in the frame is the players and the glossy, dripping paint they lay down.
styles.ownable: The painters keep the original MS-Paint DNA: a box head, two dot eyes, a flat-line mouth and a flat cap with a brim. They are redrawn as bold, confident cartoon figures rather than replaced, so the game keeps the identity it already had. The contrast in medium is the hook. Nobody pairs Saturday-morning cartoon painters with a Chinese/Japanese ink-wash landscape (ensō sun, misted mountains, floating crags, pine and bamboo), so players have no ready comparison the way they would with pixel art. The colour rule is also a game mechanic. Because the world is strictly greyscale, any saturated pixel is either a player or paint. That makes the score (painted surface) and team ownership readable at a glance, even at quarter-pane split-screen size, and every team palette (blue/orange, pink/green, blue/yellow) pops equally against grey. Paint is "dropped colour on a monochrome scroll", which is a strong thematic image for a game about covering the world in colour.
styles.self:
**What works:**
- The mix reads instantly: grey ink-wash world, colourful cartoon players and paint.
- At 480x270 both players, the spray arc and every painted segment stay clearly legible, and the backdrop drops away as intended.
- The ink medium is convincing: crags fading into mist, misty mountain ridges, the dry-brush ensō, bleeding pine and bamboo.
- The characters are appealing and carry the original box-head-and-flat-cap identity forward.
- The sheet shows idle/run/jump for both teams, both weapons large, surface swatches (bare, sprayed, rolled, contested) and a 1:1 in-game-scale lineup in all five palettes.

**Weaknesses:**
- The characters are a fairly conventional clean vector-cartoon style. The originality comes from the pairing, not from the figure drawing, and on their own they could look like generic flash-game characters.
- The style clash is intentional but some viewers may read it as unresolved rather than designed. The ink linework and the cartoon outline are both black, which helps tie them together.
- Hand-weapon contact is approximate: the sprayer grip sits slightly off the hand in the run pose, and the large roller's crank frame is hard to see.
- The scene's lower middle band is a bit empty.
- The ramp's unpainted section is a thin hatched line rather than a solid slab.
- There is a real risk of overlap with a pure 'sumi' concept on the environment side. What sets this one apart is the bold cartoon characters and glossy outlined paint.
comps: de Blob (a grey world that you colour in is the core comparison for the premise)
Okami / Sumioni: Demon Arts (sumi-e ink world)
Gris / Hue / MadWorld (colour-on-monochrome as a mechanic)
Castle Crashers / BattleBlock Theater / Newgrounds Flash cartoons (the figure drawing)
Mark of the Ninja / Shank (thick-outline 2D cartoon characters)
styles.anim: The flat fills, uniform outlines and simple limbs suit a cutout or bone rig (Spine/DragonBones, or the engine's own sprite parts). A rig would give idle, run, jump and fire for two weapons with about a dozen parts per character. Alternatively, 6-8 frame hand-drawn cycles at 12fps with a 2-3 frame line boil would sell the hand-made feel and hide stiff tweening. Mid-tier cost: cheaper than 16-bit pixel art at this detail level, much dearer than the MS-Paint originals. The weapon-hand contact problems in this sheet (the idle sprayer floats off the hand, and the roller frame is nearly invisible in the jump pose) are exactly what a rig magnifies, so lock the grip points early. The environment barely animates: drifting mist, a slow parallax layer and the occasional bamboo sway. Paint needs drip and splash sprites.
styles.engine: Good. The characters split cleanly into greyscale tint masks (cap, overalls, reservoir paint, roller sleeve) plus a fixed black outline and skin/white layer. The sheet already shows five palettes from one design. The ink-wash world should be pre-painted static layers: scanned or AI-assisted sumi textures for the parallax backdrop, plus tileable crag-top strips and crag bodies. Do NOT reproduce the SVG feTurbulence/displacement filters at runtime. A multiply paper-grain overlay is a cheap full-screen pass and is optional. The only real shader cost is the paint: the look depends on unioned paint shapes with one shared black outline and white gloss. That needs either an outline pass on the paint-coverage mask (dilate/SDF edge in the paint compositor) or pre-outlined decal stamps that merge badly when they overlap. Drips at ledge edges can be a sprite library triggered by coverage near an edge. Watch the engine's painted-surface representation: here paint is a raised band sitting ON the ledge line, so coverage has to read as a thickness strip along platform tops, not a recolour of the existing surface.
strengths: The colour rule is a gameplay rule. With a strictly greyscale world, every saturated pixel is a player or score, and the 480x270 pane proves it: both painters, the arc and all six paint segments read instantly.
Paint contrast stays strong across all palettes, because black-outlined paint stays legible even for yellow on pale paper.
Sprayer splatter and roller band leave visibly different marks, which is good for reading who painted what.
The environment is forgiving: ink wash is meant to be loose and blurry, so a non-artist (or AI-assisted) backdrop reads as intentional rather than amateur.
The floating crags, with one dark top stroke marking the walkable surface, separate collision from decoration well.
The world as a monochrome scroll that the players colour in is a strong, marketable thematic image.
risks: The characters are the weak link. They read as generic vector Flash-game painters (Castle Crashers/BattleBlock adjacent), not as the MS-Paint box-heads. The head has become a rounded cartoon face with a cap, and most of the original's weird charm is gone. The identity claim of 'keeps the MS-Paint DNA' is overstated.
de Blob already owns 'paint colour back into a grey world'. The ink-wash framing makes it fresher, but reviewers will make that comparison.
The style clash may read as two asset packs glued together. Crisp vector characters over soft wet ink have nothing tying them together except the black line colour.

At in-scene size the characters are small (about 12% of frame height). At quarter-pane they read mostly through their caps and overalls. Facial expression, the main selling point of 'expressive cartoon', is lost.

The paint is drawn as a raised band floating on top of ledges, with drips. It needs an outline/union pass in the paint renderer to look like this, and naive overlapping decals will break the shared silhouette.

Execution defects in the concept: the sprayer hand grip is off, the roller crank and handle are hard to read in the jump pose, the ramp's bare section is a thin hatched line rather than a slab, and the lower middle of the scene is empty.
Greyscale levels risk visual monotony across many stages. Variety must come from composition and motif (bamboo, pine, ensō, waterfalls) rather than palette.
styles.verdict: This is the strongest gameplay-readability proposition I'd expect among these concepts: a grey ink world plus saturated outlined paint makes score and team ownership readable at a glance in a quarter pane, and the environment half is cheap and forgiving for a solo developer. The weakness is the characters. As executed, they are competent but generic vector cartoon painters that have dropped most of the crude box-head identity the author valued, so the style's ownability currently rests on the pairing alone. Worth pursuing if the painters are pushed back toward the weirder, flatter MS-Paint silhouette (true box heads, stiffer stick limbs, fat outlines) rather than polished toward Flash-game appeal.

identity.reason: I checked the render. It reads very well and the world is attractive, but the characters have become generic Flash-cartoon painters with rounded faces and skin. The soul of the original is gone, and the premise of colouring a grey world invites a comparison with de Blob.

production.reason: Best paint readability of the set, and the ink-wash environments forgive a lot. But clean outlined cartoon characters must be drawn competently across every animation, and the shared outline on paint needs an SDF/dilate pass. That costs more than the crude styles.

player.reason: Best in the set when I looked at the 480x270 pane. The world is strictly grey, and the paint is black-outlined with drips, so every painted segment and both players read at once. The outline also protects yellow and green on pale paper, and the sheet shows all five palettes holding up. The thick-outlined figures stay legible as figures in a quarter pane, not just as coloured tokens. Bold colour on misty ink would also make a strong Steam capsule. Weak spot: the characters have drifted toward a generic Flash cartoon.

identity.reason: I checked the workshop reference. It is competent, dense 16-bit art, but its generic cap-and-overalls guys could come from any indie pixel brawler. That is exactly the comparison trap the author wants to avoid. The busy backdrop competes with the paint, and the original stick-figure identity is completely gone. A solo non-artist cannot hold that bar consistently.

production.reason: The reference is dense, detailed 16-bit art: lit props, signage and characters with shading ramps. A solo non-artist cannot match that across 4+ arenas, multiple characters and animation states. The comparison field (Celeste, Dead Cells and hundreds of others) is the harshest of any option, and rough execution shows immediately.

player.reason: Strongest trailer appeal and polish as a still. As a player lens it fails readability: dense props, warm lighting and saturated barrels compete with the paint, there is orange and blue in the background, and it invites direct comparison with every polished pixel game. It is also a large production bar.

panel.mix:
Use Paint.exe figures on a riso-printed world, tuned to fix the flaws I could see in the renders.
(1) Keep the author's figures exactly as drawn: aliased white fill, black 3px line, team tint only on the cap, tank, roller sleeve and speckle. Oversize the figures and weapons about 1.3-1.5x for quarter-pane size.
(2) Change the riso key ink from navy to a warm charcoal or near-black, keeping navy only as a faint second ink. That stops blue paint and the blue team vanishing into the world (visible in the mix render's spray arc), and it also fixes the doodle concept's blue-on-blue-ink problem.
(3) Keep cream, lightly halftoned walkable tops, as in mix_mspaint_riso, so paint always sits on a mid-light surface. Put a thin dark keyline under the paint so yellow survives.
(4) Borrow from the mspaint concept the deliberate self-aware background gags ('do not move this cloud', a WET sign), printed in the second ink at low contrast, so the world has personality without noise.
(5) Make the paper grain a screen-space pass that weakens at quarter-pane size, and bake world-locked halftone at integer scale.
This keeps the soul (his literal figure), makes the crudeness read as deliberate through a crafted frame, has almost no direct comparison, is cheap (he can draw the figures in Paint), and shares the existing menu art's halftone and splatter language. That means the UI pass the user wants to do second becomes a matching job, not a redesign.
avoid: mix_pixel_collage: the painters read as Mario knock-offs, which brings back the pixel comparison trap
sticker / mix_sticker_drafting: they sand the box-head into generic mobile-mascot art, which is the identity loss the author fears
mix_cartoon_ink: the most readable layout, but the characters lose the original soul (rounded faces, Flash-cartoon look)
gouache and mix_sketch_gouache: painted backdrops are the skill a solo non-artist lacks, and both renders come out muddy
pixel_baseline: competent but generic, with the most famous comparison field in indie games
Any direction where team-hue world ink (navy/blue) sits directly under blue team paint without a separation rule
panel.notes:
I viewed the full-size scenes for mix_mspaint_riso, riso, mspaint, doodle, drafting, geometric, linocut, chalk, sumi, mix_cartoon_ink and the pixel reference, the small renders for mix_mspaint_riso, mspaint, riso and doodle, and the mix_mspaint_riso character sheet. The renders confirmed these critique claims:
- mix_mspaint_riso: blue spray loses contrast over navy at 480x270, and the grain reads as static.
- riso: the even halftone wall flattens to a grey buzz.
- doodle: blue paint merges with the blue ballpoint outlines.
- drafting: platforms are faint.
- mix_cartoon_ink: the figures have drifted to generic cartoon.

On the identity lens, the top four (the riso mix, riso, mspaint, doodle) form one cluster: the author's literal figure in a frame that makes crude look deliberate. They differ mainly in how strong that frame is. Riso wins on frame strength and on continuity with the existing menu art, which matters for the user's sequencing (gameplay look first, then the UI made to match).

The panel should treat the key-ink colour as an open decision. Navy matches the menu art, but it sits on the blue team's hue. Charcoal with a navy second ink keeps the menu link and removes that conflict. One more thing worth prototyping early is world-locked halftone under camera scroll, because shimmer there could sink every riso variant.

panel.mix: Use Paint.exe rules for characters and paint, on a neutral graphite world. The characters are the original aliased box-head flat-cap figures, drawn at about 1.5x line weight, with an oversized cap and weapon so they read at quarter pane. Paint is flat bucket-fill bands with jagged edges and drip sprites, with no gloss shader. The world takes doodle's quiet notebook calm but in grey or black pencil, never blue ink, so no team pair loses its edge. Slabs are mid-grey with a dark top edge so walkable geometry reads. It ships with zero load-bearing shaders: point sampling, integer scale and a pixel-snapped camera. Every asset can be made in a raster editor, and four arenas are slab layouts plus one or two gag props each. It also gives the later UI pass an obvious language to match: the Paint window chrome, the tool palette as weapon select and the colour swatches as team pick. That fits the user's plan to fix gameplay first and then bring the UI in line.
avoid: pixel_baseline: the detailed 16-bit bar is unreachable for one non-artist at consistent quality across 4+ arenas
Any direction whose identity lives in a runtime shader the d3d11 path doesn't have yet (gouache impasto, stainedglass emissive/bloom, sticker die-cut dilation, popart screen-space Ben-Day)
Full-screen grain or halftone that turns to static at 480x270 (mix_mspaint_riso grain, riso wall) unless it is cut back per pane
Blue world ink or navy backgrounds behind a team that can be blue (doodle, mix_mspaint_riso)
Cream or kraft worlds without a dark rim on yellow paint, since the blue/yellow pair is untested in almost every concept
Polishing the box-head into generic vector mascots (mix_sticker_drafting, mix_cartoon_ink characters)
panel.notes: I viewed the scene_small renders for doodle, mspaint, riso, chalk, geometric, mix_cartoon_ink, mix_mspaint_riso and linocut, plus the pixel workshop reference. Seen from the production side, the crude family (mspaint, doodle, riso, geometric) clusters at the top because roughness reads as style there and none of them needs a load-bearing shader. mspaint edges out doodle for three reasons: its quarter-pane render is the cleanest, its paint works as flat fills with no gloss pass, and it has no blue-on-blue ink clash. Geometric has the most legible figures at small size and would be my pick if the author trusts his layout and palette sense. Every concept still has stick limbs that dissolve at quarter pane, so the first production test, whatever style wins, should be thicker character lines or bigger caps and weapons at 1x, with all three team pairs (especially yellow) tested on actual surfaces.

panel.mix: Keep mix_cartoon_ink's grey sumi world and its black-outlined, union-shaped glossy paint, which makes every team pair readable, yellow included. Change two things. First, take linocut's solid near-black ink slabs as the walkable ledges, so every painted surface sits on the darkest value and the walkable surface stays unambiguous at 480x270. Second, push the characters back to the original MS-Paint geometry: a true box head, a flat cap, and stiff stick-ish limbs, but drawn with the fat cartoon outline and filled team-colour overalls so they stay readable as bodies in a quarter pane. The result is a grey ink world, dark ledges, fat-outlined box-head painters, and outlined paint as the only colour. It reads instantly in 4-way split, it holds up for pink/green and blue/yellow, and it gives a striking capsule (bold colour slashing across a monochrome scroll) without the Flash-mascot genericness or the pixel-art comparison trap. For the UI pass that follows, use the same rule: monochrome ink frames with a team-colour accent.
avoid: Any team-hue world tint (blue ballpoint ink, navy key ink with blue team, teal chalk floor, olive/rust props, kraft/ochre grounds): it kills one colour pair
Cream or white bare surfaces as the main paint base without an outline: yellow disappears
Thin paint strips (stained glass, pixel collage): coverage must read as territory at 480x270
Full-frame halftone, paper grain or noise overlays at pane size: they turn to static and shimmer in split-screen
Hairline stick figures with no fill: players become specks in a quarter pane
Dense, warmly lit prop backgrounds like the pixel baseline, which compete with paint for attention
Paint that reads as tape or stickers rather than splatter
panel.notes: I viewed the 480x270 scene_small renders for mix_cartoon_ink, riso, chalk, linocut, geometric, sumi, sticker, mspaint, mix_mspaint_riso, doodle, mix_sketch_gouache and popart, plus the mix_cartoon_ink character sheet and the pixel workshop reference. Two things predicted quarter-pane readability most strongly. One is a dark value under the paint (linocut, cartoon_ink, riso, chalk, geometric). The other is filled bodies or outlined figures rather than hairline sticks. Paint with a black outline is the only treatment I saw that protects yellow on light grounds, which suits the user's 'gameplay style first' order: settle that paint and ledge rule now, and the UI can inherit the ink-frame language afterwards. The pixel baseline wins the still-image beauty contest, but it loses on the things this game is scored on.
